claims.title: No public-domain oral tradition
claims.content: The authors state that the Enneagram's type information was not passed down in a public-domain oral tradition.

claims.title: Enneagram arrival in United States
claims.content: The Enneagram came to the United States around 1970.

claims.title: Enneagram of personality defined
claims.content: The Enneagram of personality is a modern synthesis of ancient and modern psychological and spiritual teachings.

claims.title: Modern Enneagram developers named
claims.content: Oscar Ichazo, Claudio Naranjo, Don Richard Riso, and Russ Hudson are among the modern developers who created the Enneagram as a synthesis.

claims.title: Enneagram ancient roots
claims.content: The modern Enneagram has ancient roots, including elements from Greek thought, the Christian Desert Fathers, Kabbalists, and Sufis.

claims.title: Instinctual Variants defined as subtypes
claims.content: Instinctual Variants are the so-called subtypes of the Enneagram types.

claims.title: Teachers differ on wings and levels
claims.content: Some Enneagram teachers teach the wings and the nine internal Levels of Development within each type, while others do not.

claims.title: No single agreed Enneagram interpretation
claims.content: There is no universally agreed interpretation of the Enneagram, only an evolving understanding of it.

claims.title: Ichazo's work underlies Enneagram
claims.content: Oscar Ichazo's work is the basis of the Enneagram system, according to the author.

claims.title: Essence friend: supportive awakening friend
claims.content: An Essence friend is a friend who supports a person in awakening, as described by Gurdjieff.

claims.title: Enneagram maps personality blockages
claims.content: The Enneagram serves as a map that shows the points of blockage in a person's particular personality structure.

claims.title: Enneagram indicates growth needs
claims.content: The Enneagram indicates what each person's personality structure needs for growth and transformation, and each type requires its own prescriptions for growth.

claims.title: Naranjo developed type psychology
claims.content: Claudio Naranjo developed the psychology of the Enneagram types, according to the author.

claims.title: Enneagram: nine personality structures
claims.content: The Enneagram is a personality system based on the premise that human nature has nine basic personality structures, each with its own attitudes, behaviors, motivations, and habits.

claims.title: Stage three: presence and awareness
claims.content: The third stage of Enneagram work is cultivating awareness or presence, which facilitates and deepens transformation.

claims.title: Spiritual practice needed for benefit
claims.content: Getting the full benefit of the Enneagram requires integrating it into a genuine spiritual practice.

claims.title: Fourth Way ideas in the book
claims.content: The book enriches its presentation of the Enneagram with ideas from Fourth Way schools and other awareness practices.

claims.title: Transformation requires presence and awareness
claims.content: Self-observation and self-understanding alone give insight, while transformation occurs only through presence and awareness.

claims.title: Information alone can entrench patterns
claims.content: Using the Enneagram only as information can solidify personality structures rather than liberate a person from them.

claims.title: Stage one: self-observation
claims.content: The first stage of Enneagram work is self-observation, which means seeing one's behavior as objectively as possible.

claims.title: Principal uses: self and others
claims.content: The two principal uses of the Enneagram are self-understanding and understanding others.

claims.title: Three stages of Enneagram work
claims.content: Three stages of Enneagram work move from self-observation to self-understanding and then to presence and awareness.

claims.title: Stage two: self-understanding
claims.content: The second stage of Enneagram work is self-understanding, which means learning the true motives for one's behavior.

claims.title: Reported spiritual rediscovery
claims.content: Many students and readers of the Enneagram report that it helped them rediscover spirituality.

claims.title: Enneagram as spiritual path
claims.content: True self-knowledge is the first step toward spirituality, and the Enneagram at its deepest is a path toward the spiritual.

claims.title: Personality: superficial self aspects
claims.content: Personality is the more superficial aspect of the self, in contrast with Essence, in Enneagram work.

claims.title: Poor judgment of character causes harm
claims.content: Without being good judges of others' characters, people can be terribly hurt and abused.

claims.title: Self-knowledge prevents harmful choices
claims.content: Without self-knowledge, people can make choices with disastrous outcomes and can harm themselves and others.

claims.title: Lack of knowledge harms marriages
claims.content: Many marriages end in bitterness and divorce because the partners do not know themselves or each other.

claims.title: Enneagram supports liberation and healing
claims.content: The Enneagram can help people become freer from whatever is blocked, negative, destructive, fearful, and wounded in themselves, and can aid their healing.

claims.title: Essence: deeper true nature
claims.content: Essence is the deeper aspect of a person's true nature, as distinguished from personality in Enneagram work.

claims.title: Enneagram as early warning system
claims.content: The Enneagram can act as an early warning system that reveals unconscious tendencies before they become self-defeating habits.

claims.title: Enneagram supports objective view of others
claims.content: Understanding the Enneagram helps people see others more objectively while staying true to their own center.

claims.title: Check implicit personality theory
claims.content: Recognizing one's implicit personality theory and making it accurate and comprehensive is helpful.

claims.title: Enneagram aids understanding of others
claims.content: The Enneagram helps people understand others, including how they think, what they fear and desire, what they value, and their strengths and weaknesses.

claims.title: Enneagram is not overtly religious
claims.content: The Enneagram is not overtly religious, and it has been adapted to many religions because it reflects patterns found in human nature.

claims.title: Ego forms block experience of Divine
claims.content: The Enneagram can describe the forms the human ego takes, which are the primary obstacles to a direct experience of the Divine.

claims.title: Everyone holds implicit personality theory
claims.content: Everyone uses an implicit personality theory, whether or not they are conscious of it, to judge how others will react and what motivates them.

claims.title: Enneagram as a discernment tool
claims.content: The Enneagram is a tool that, when used properly, helps people distinguish their personalities, the more superficial aspects of themselves, from their Essence, the deeper aspects of their true nature.

claims.title: Enneagram value depends on use
claims.content: The Enneagram is only as useful as a reader makes it, and it enriches people to the degree they understand it correctly and use it properly.

claims.title: Enneagram reveals personality pitfalls
claims.content: The Enneagram shows where a person's personality most often trips them up, which gives them more psychological space to maneuver.

claims.title: Type recognition reveals hidden traits
claims.content: Recognizing one's personality type and seeing it at work reveals hidden aspects of personality, which can begin to loosen up.

claims.title: Type qualities and nonjudgment
claims.content: A personality type has both positive and negative qualities, and people should neither exalt nor condemn their type or use it to judge others.

claims.title: Book excludes basic theory and profiles
claims.content: Understanding the Enneagram does not cover the basic structure and theory of the Enneagram or full descriptions of the nine personality types.

claims.title: Childhood messages to hide self
claims.content: Children can come to believe that parts of themselves are not safe to show to the world, based on messages from their parents.

claims.title: Parents limited by own gaps
claims.content: Parents who had their own developmental gaps and losses could not fully support the unfolding of all aspects of their child's Essence, even when they loved the child.

claims.title: Personality as childhood defenses
claims.content: Personality is largely a collection of internal defenses, reactions, and deeply ingrained beliefs and habits formed in the past, particularly in childhood.

claims.title: Essence as spiritual core
claims.content: Essence, the spiritual core of a person, is the True Nature that people can reexperience by exploring their personality's defenses.

claims.title: Cross-referenced to Personality Types
claims.content: Understanding the Enneagram is cross-referenced to the Revised Edition of Personality Types.

claims.title: Mistaken identity with personality
claims.content: People suffer from mistaken identity: they forget their True Nature and believe they are their personality.

claims.title: Type as core experience pattern
claims.content: Personality type is the core pattern by which a person organizes and interprets experience.

claims.title: Central problem is estrangement
claims.content: Every person faces one central problem, estrangement from their deepest nature, regardless of personality type or ego form.

claims.title: Personality attachment blocks true nature
claims.content: The Enneagram identifies the main blockages between a person and their true nature, which are attachments to their personality.

claims.title: Book builds on Ichazo and Naranjo
claims.content: Understanding the Enneagram is a practical guide to the Enneagram system that builds on insights first presented by Oscar Ichazo and Claudio Naranjo.

claims.title: Present attention expands awareness
claims.content: Returning attention to the present moment causes awareness to expand beyond the narrow concerns of personality.

claims.title: Personality hides Essential nature
claims.content: Personality forms as a survival adjustment to caregivers, and this process gradually hides a person's Essential nature.

claims.title: Awareness interrupts reactive momentum
claims.content: Awareness can interrupt the momentum of personality-driven reactions and prevent harmful outcomes.

claims.title: Awareness: registers and pays attention
claims.content: Awareness is the aspect of Being that registers experience, and it is also a person's capacity to pay attention.

claims.title: Personality (as used here)
claims.content: Personality is the set of habitual reactions, self-image, and beliefs that a person identifies with, formed as adjustments to early caregivers.

claims.title: Attention narrows into personality
claims.content: Attention is usually drawn into personality preoccupations such as fantasies, anxieties, and reactions, which narrows awareness.

claims.title: Identifying with personality reactions
claims.content: People tend to identify with their habitual reactions and self-image, and they often avoid looking beneath their personality.

claims.title: True Self differs from personality
claims.content: The true Self and the personality are different, and presence restores a proper balance between them.

claims.title: Early pain shapes later interpretation
claims.content: Painful early childhood experiences shape how people interpret later events, which reinforces their early sense of self.

claims.title: Presence cannot be automated
claims.content: Presence never becomes habitual, so no formula or technique can keep a person present at all times.

claims.title: Type One traits
claims.content: Type One, the Reformer, is principled, purposeful, self-controlled, and perfectionistic.

claims.title: Enneagram as dynamic system
claims.content: The Enneagram is a dynamic personality system whose nine types are interrelated, not static categories.

claims.title: Enneagram's primary purpose
claims.content: The primary use of the Enneagram is to help people discover their true nature and the obstacles to expressing it.

claims.title: Type Six traits
claims.content: Type Six, the Loyalist, is reliable, committed, defensive, and suspicious.

claims.title: Type Seven traits
claims.content: Type Seven, the Enthusiast, is spontaneous, versatile, distractible, and excessive.

claims.title: Type Four traits
claims.content: Type Four, the Individualist, is expressive, romantic, withholding, and temperamental.

claims.title: Personality runs on awareness
claims.content: Personality operates automatically when a person is unaware of it, and awareness reduces its automatic patterns.

claims.title: Essence (True Self) definition
claims.content: Essence, also called the True Self, is the deeper inner nature of a person, distinct from the automatic self of personality.

claims.title: Type Three traits
claims.content: Type Three, the Achiever, is adaptable, ambitious, image-conscious, and arrogant.

claims.title: Type Five traits
claims.content: Type Five, the Investigator, is innovative, cerebral, detached, and provocative.

claims.title: Type Two traits
claims.content: Type Two, the Helper, is generous, demonstrative, people-pleasing, and possessive.

claims.title: Enneagram types one to seven
claims.content: The Enneagram's short descriptions characterize Types One through Seven, each with four traits.

claims.title: Nine Enneagram personality types
claims.content: The Enneagram describes nine distinct personality types, each a different way human nature expresses itself.

claims.title: Individuals differ within a type
claims.content: Individuals within the same personality type can be distinguished from one another, as shades within one color family can be told apart.

claims.title: Shared traits in personality disorders
claims.content: People with the same common personality disorder resemble one another in their thoughts, speech, and responses, as depressives resemble other depressives.

claims.title: Types as general patterns
claims.content: Personality types are general patterns, and each individual is a unique variation on those patterns.

claims.title: Type Nine Peacemaker traits
claims.content: Type Nine, the Peacemaker, is reassuring, agreeable, disengaged, and stubborn.

claims.title: Choosing the desired type
claims.content: A common problem when finding one's Enneagram type is choosing the type one would like to be rather than the type one actually is.

claims.title: Arica presentation type names
claims.content: The Arica presentation names the personality types after their ego fixations, such as calling the One Ego Resentment.

claims.title: Uniqueness from personal history
claims.content: Individual uniqueness comes from each person's unique history, while membership in a personality type comes from shared traits.

claims.title: Types are distinct categories
claims.content: Different personality types are distinct categories, so a Five is not an Eight and an Eight is not a One.

claims.title: Type Eight Challenger traits
claims.content: Type Eight, the Challenger, is self-confident, decisive, dominating, and confrontational.

claims.title: Basic personality type meaning
claims.content: A person's basic personality type is the type that stands out most as typical of that person, though a little of every type may be found in each person.

claims.title: Shared human nature and uniqueness
claims.content: Human beings share a common biological and psychological basis, and the Enneagram does not deny individual uniqueness.

claims.title: Enneagram personality types
claims.content: The Enneagram is a system of personality types that describes general patterns, which individuals vary from.

claims.title: Type names reflect healthy traits
claims.content: The Enneagram type names reflect traits of each type that are relatively healthy.

claims.title: Weakness linked to strength
claims.content: In each personality type, the most important weakness is related to, but not the same as, the most important strength.

claims.title: Type description balance
claims.content: Type descriptions must be specific enough to convey precise information about each type and general enough to include all individuals of that type.

claims.title: Type label as general class
claims.content: Calling someone a Five gives a general class, like calling an object red, and each type contains hundreds of possible individual variations.

claims.title: Types are not arbitrary
claims.content: Enneagram personality types are not arbitrary; their traits grow out of each other and express basic fears, desires, and needs.

claims.title: Feeling Triad types and issues
claims.content: The Feeling Triad consists of Types Two, Three, and Four, and its issues involve finding value and identity.

claims.title: Six overthinks and seeks reassurance
claims.content: The Six is the primary type of the Thinking Triad, is most out of touch with inner guidance, and overthinks while looking to beliefs or trusted others for reassurance.

claims.title: Triad inner dialectical structure
claims.content: In each Enneagram Triad, one type overexpresses the Triad's center, another underexpresses it, and the third is most out of touch with it.

claims.title: Type identification needs pattern
claims.content: Identifying one's Enneagram type from a single trait is almost impossible; the larger pattern of traits and motivations must be considered.

claims.title: Enneagram Triad definition
claims.content: An Enneagram Triad is one of three groups of three types that share one center of human intelligence as the basis of their personality structure.

claims.title: Seven jumps between thoughts
claims.content: The Seven underexpresses thinking and jumps quickly from one thought to another, or from thinking into doing, without thinking through consequences.

claims.title: Instinctive Triad types and issues
claims.content: The Instinctive Triad consists of Types Eight, Nine, and One, and its issues involve relating to instinctual energy in a balanced way.

claims.title: Three is out of touch with feelings
claims.content: The Three is the primary type of the Feeling Triad, is most out of touch with its feelings, and is motivated by a desire to be valued and accepted.

claims.title: Triads linked to intelligence centers
claims.content: Each Enneagram Triad is associated with one center of human intelligence: Thinking, Feeling, or Instinctive.

claims.title: Enneagram center definition
claims.content: An Enneagram center is one of three functions of human intelligence (Thinking, Feeling, or Instinctive), also called the head, heart, and gut centers.

claims.title: Four underexpresses feelings
claims.content: The Four underexpresses feelings, is painfully self-conscious, and is the dialectical opposite of the Two.

claims.title: Nine Enneagram types in Triads
claims.content: The Enneagram has nine personality types grouped into three Triads of three types each.

claims.title: Two overexpresses feelings
claims.content: The Two overexpresses feelings, becoming effusive and overly friendly while repressing awareness of its own needs or ulterior motives.

claims.title: Thinking Triad types and issues
claims.content: The Thinking Triad consists of Types Five, Six, and Seven, and its issues involve finding inner guidance and support.

claims.title: Five overexpresses thinking
claims.content: The Five overexpresses thinking, is the most cerebral and mentally intense type, and lives for ideas while neglecting practical aspects of life.

claims.title: Eight overexpresses instinctual energy
claims.content: Eight is the type in the Instinctive Triad that overexpresses its instinctual energy.

claims.title: Type is a range on the circle
claims.content: A type is a range of points along its segment of the Enneagram circle, and a personality crystallizes at a point in that range.

claims.title: Basic type does not change
claims.content: The authors are convinced that people do not change from one basic personality type to another.

claims.title: One underexpresses instinctual energy
claims.content: One underexpresses its instinctual energy, mainly by trying to control it.

claims.title: Three types share insecurity and anxiety
claims.content: Three types share problems with insecurity and anxiety, expressed differently and with different causes.

claims.title: Closer to a type means stronger wing
claims.content: A personality that crystallizes closer to an adjacent type has a stronger wing toward that type.

claims.title: Wing theory is disputed
claims.content: Writers disagree about wings: some say there is no wing, some say there is usually one dominant wing, and others say there are two wings.

claims.title: Wing defined as adjacent type
claims.content: A wing is the type adjacent to a person's basic type, which provides other psychological functions that sometimes complement and sometimes oppose the basic type.

claims.title: Nine is most out of touch
claims.content: Nine is the primary type of the Instinctive Triad and is the type most out of touch with its instinctual energy.

claims.title: Basic type shaped by childhood
claims.content: A person's basic type reflects genetics and childhood experiences, especially relationships with parents.

claims.title: Emotional shifts follow predictable patterns
claims.content: People shift emotional states many times a day in recognizable patterns, which the inner lines of the Enneagram can predict.

claims.title: Authors see one dominant wing
claims.content: The Enneagram authors' view is that most people have one dominant wing, while some people seem to have both wings or no wings.

claims.title: Triad types share aggression and repression
claims.content: The three types of the Instinctive Triad share aggression and repression, though these issues are expressed differently and have different causes.

claims.title: Ichazo founded Arica School
claims.content: Oscar Ichazo created the Arica School to transmit the knowledge he had received, teaching in Chile in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

claims.title: One's stress and relaxed moves
claims.content: A One under stress moves to Four, and a One who is more relaxed moves to Seven.

claims.title: Four types for full analysis
claims.content: Four personality types are pertinent for a full analysis of any individual: the basic type, the wing, the type in the Direction of Integration, and the type in the Direction of Disintegration.

claims.title: Disintegration signals overtaxed coping
claims.content: The Direction of Disintegration, also called stress, signals that a person is under increased stress and that the normal coping mechanisms of the basic type are being overtaxed.

claims.title: Nine's secure and stress moves
claims.content: A Nine moves to Three when more secure and to Six under greater stress.

claims.title: Integration signals greater security
claims.content: The Direction of Integration signals that a person is more secure and can mark further integration of the basic type.

claims.title: Nine Levels of Development
claims.content: People fluctuate among the traits of their type along a continuum of nine Levels of Development, from high-functioning states to painful, potentially pathological ones.

claims.title: Direction of Integration sequences
claims.content: The Direction of Integration of the Enneagram runs through the sequence 1-7-5-8-2-4-1 and 9-3-6-9.

claims.title: Ichazo originated the Enneagram
claims.content: Oscar Ichazo put together the Enneagram of Personality Types as a modern synthesis of ancient wisdom traditions.

claims.title: 1970 Arica study group
claims.content: In 1970, a group including Claudio Naranjo and John Lilly studied with Oscar Ichazo in Arica, Chile, for several weeks.

claims.title: Direction of Disintegration sequences
claims.content: The Direction of Disintegration (stress) of the Enneagram runs through the sequence 1-4-2-8-5-7-1 and 9-6-3-9.

claims.title: Traditional Enneagram dates 1960s
claims.content: The traditional Enneagram dates to the 1960s, when Ichazo first taught it.

claims.title: Chief feature definition
claims.content: The chief feature is the linchpin of a person's ego structure, the basic characteristic that defines them.

claims.title: Nine forms to seven sins unknown
claims.content: How the original nine Divine Forms became reduced to seven deadly sins remains unexplained.

claims.title: Ichazo's 108 Enneagrams
claims.content: Ichazo taught Arican students a system of 108 Enneagrams, while the American Enneagram movement is based mainly on four of them.

claims.title: Desert Fathers and seven sins
claims.content: Early Christian Desert Fathers studied the loss of the Divine Forms in ego consciousness, and the distortions of those forms came to be known as the seven deadly sins.

claims.title: Gurdjieff taught no Enneagram types
claims.content: Gurdjieff did not teach a system of character types associated with the Enneagram symbol.

claims.title: Misattribution of nine-type system
claims.content: Many early Enneagram enthusiasts mistakenly attributed the nine-type system to Gurdjieff or to the Sufis.

claims.title: Ichazo created nine-type system
claims.content: The nine-type Enneagram system is Oscar Ichazo's creation, combining traditions he drew on rather than an ancient oral tradition.

claims.title: Enneagram symbol ancient origins
claims.content: The Enneagram symbol can be traced back at least as far as Pythagoras.

claims.title: Tree of Life purpose
claims.content: The Tree of Life is said to map the patterns and laws by which God created the manifest universe.

claims.title: Enneagram purpose: Essence and ego
claims.content: Ichazo designed the Enneagram system primarily to clarify the relationship between Essence and personality, or ego.

claims.title: Four Enneagrams used in America
claims.content: The American Enneagram movement is based primarily on four of Ichazo's Enneagrams: the Passions, the Virtues, the Fixations, and the Holy Ideas.

claims.title: Nine Divine Forms origin
claims.content: Ichazo drew on the idea of nine Divine Forms, which Plato discussed as the Divine Forms or Platonic Solids.

claims.title: Gurdjieff revealed chief feature
claims.content: Gurdjieff revealed to advanced students what he called their chief feature.

claims.title: Ichazo's view of Essence and ego
claims.content: In Ichazo's view, every person is perfect, fearless, and in loving unity with the cosmos in essence, and the ego's development causes a fall into personality.

claims.title: Plotinus on Divine Forms
claims.content: Plotinus discussed the idea of nine Divine Forms in his work The Enneads, developed in the third century by Neo-Platonic philosophers.

claims.title: Gurdjieff reintroduced Enneagram symbol
claims.content: George Gurdjieff reintroduced the Enneagram symbol to the modern world and taught it through sacred dances or movements.

claims.title: Tree of Life diagram structure
claims.content: The Tree of Life in Kabbalah is a diagram of ten spheres (Sefirot) connected by twenty-two paths.

claims.title: Enneagram examines distortion of Essence
claims.content: Ichazo saw the Enneagram as a means to examine how the soul qualities of Essence become distorted into ego states.

claims.title: Enneagram philosophical influences
claims.content: The philosophy behind the Enneagram contains components from mystical Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Taoism, Buddhism, and ancient Greek philosophy.

claims.title: Recognizing type distortions
claims.content: Recognizing one's characteristic Passion and ego fixation can help a person recognize the obscured Essence quality.

claims.title: Nine ways of losing center
claims.content: Ichazo's theory holds that there are nine main ways people lose their center and forget their connection with the Divine.

claims.title: Holy Ideas defined
claims.content: In Oscar Ichazo's Enneagram, Holy Ideas are the essential qualities of the higher mind, specific nondual perspectives of Essence.

claims.title: Passions defined
claims.content: In Oscar Ichazo's Enneagram, a Passion is the ego's emotional coping strategy after a person loses contact with a Virtue.

claims.title: Virtue transforms Passion
claims.content: Recalling a Virtue in a state of presence can gradually transform its corresponding Passion.

claims.title: Virtues defined
claims.content: In Oscar Ichazo's Enneagram, Virtues are essential qualities of the heart that people experience when they abide in Essence.

claims.title: Enneagram linked to three centers
claims.content: Ichazo related the Enneagram symbol to three Centers of human intelligence: Thinking, Feeling, and Instinct.

claims.title: Ego fixations defined
claims.content: In Oscar Ichazo's Enneagram, an ego fixation is the loss of awareness of a Holy Idea, which produces a particular delusion about the self or reality.

claims.title: Deceit defined as presenting false images
claims.content: Deceit is the tendency to believe one is the assumed self of personality rather than Essence, presenting images of oneself to cover loss of contact with Being.

claims.title: Deceit means inauthenticity, not lying
claims.content: Deceit in this sense does not necessarily mean overt lying; it means being inauthentic instead of honest and real with someone.

claims.title: Pride denies loss of Essence
claims.content: Pride is a fundamental denial of the loss of contact with Essence, particularly the loss of contact with qualities of real love.

claims.title: Holy Will defined as the one Will
claims.content: Holy Will is the recognition that there is only one Will and one unfolding reality, and that the ego only thinks it makes things happen.

claims.title: Pride seeks admiration for goodness
claims.content: Type Two pride makes goodness call attention to itself, so the person seeks to be admired, praised, rewarded, or repaid.

claims.title: Type Two fixation is ego flattery
claims.content: The fixation of Type Two is ego flattery: Twos flatter people, serve others' needs, and make others feel good to gain approval and appreciation.

claims.title: Type Two passion: pride
claims.content: The Passion of Type Two is Pride, also called Vainglory, which is caused by the loss of the Virtue of humility.

claims.title: Type Three virtue and fixation
claims.content: The Virtue of Type Three is Truthfulness and Authenticity, its Fixation is Vanity, and its Holy Idea is Holy Law and Holy Hope.

claims.title: Vainglory defined as pride in goodness
claims.content: Vainglory is pride in one's own goodness, taking special satisfaction in seeing oneself only as a loving, well-intentioned person.

claims.title: Holy Freedom defined as release from ego
claims.content: Holy Freedom is freedom from the ego and from the compulsive need to prop up the ego by being good, felt as exhilaration and openness when experiencing oneself as part of the unfolding Divine Will.

claims.title: Healthy Twos help without self-congratulation
claims.content: Healthy Type Two people help others unselfishly, without thoughts of self-congratulation, responding spontaneously and freely to a need or not responding.

claims.title: Humility defined as Being without self-reflecting
claims.content: Humility is Being without self-reflecting, in which identity does not depend on others' approval or one's own self-regard, and it is not self-disparagement.

claims.title: Type Three passion: deceit
claims.content: The Passion of Type Three is Deceit (untruthfulness), which results from the loss of the Virtue of Truthfulness.

claims.title: Pride hides pain and need
claims.content: Type Two pride includes an inability to admit hurting or neediness, and it prevents showing needs or trying to get something from others.

claims.title: Pride casts ego as essential to others
claims.content: Type Two pride causes a person to see their ego self as the most important source of love and goodness in others' lives.

claims.title: Type Two pattern: giving to get
claims.content: The general pattern of Type Two is giving in order to get, with the hope that others will notice and return positive attention.

claims.title: Type Three virtue: truthfulness
claims.content: Truthfulness (authenticity) is the virtue of the Enneagram Type Three.

claims.title: Type Four traits summary
claims.content: The Enneagram Type Four has the passion of envy, the virtues of equanimity and emotional balance, the fixation of melancholy, and the Holy Idea of Holy Origin.

claims.title: Average Threes: image over identity
claims.content: Average Threes tend to develop an image and polished package instead of their authentic feelings and identity.

claims.title: Holy Law: unified unfolding reality
claims.content: Holy Law is the perception that reality is a dynamic, unfolding unity in which no independent doing or accomplishment occurs.

claims.title: Vanity: self-image investment examples
claims.content: Vanity leads people to invest energy in building their self-image, such as through career success, favorable self-presentation, awards, or achievements.

claims.title: Holy Idea: correcting ego's doing
claims.content: Holy Idea is the perspective that corrects the ego's false perception that it is the source of doing and accomplishing.

claims.title: Holy Hope: resting in being
claims.content: Holy Hope gives confidence to rest in being and lets the ego mind stop its endless agendas and projects.

claims.title: Type Three fixation: vanity
claims.content: Vanity is the fixation of the Enneagram Type Three, described as the ego's effort to make the personality feel real and valuable.

claims.title: Type Five passion: avarice
claims.content: The passion of Enneagram Type Five is avarice.

claims.title: Envy causes alienation from others
claims.content: Envy alienates people from others and from life, leaving them feeling like outsiders who never belong.

claims.title: Fours identify with their woundedness
claims.content: Enneagram Fours identify with their sense of inner deficiency and build a lifestyle and identity around their suffering.

claims.title: Equanimity supports presence in pain
claims.content: Equanimity lets people stay present with painful experiences without being swept away by emotional reactions.

claims.title: Type Four passion: envy
claims.content: The passion of Enneagram Type Four is envy.

claims.title: Avarice origin in childhood
claims.content: Avarice arose in childhood when people lost contact with their essential natures and felt small and helpless in a vast, uncaring universe.

claims.title: Fixated Fours build victim histories
claims.content: Fixated Fours create elaborate personal histories that reinforce the belief that they have been uniquely victimized.

claims.title: Type Four fixation: melancholy
claims.content: The fixation of Enneagram Type Four is melancholy, also called fantasizing.

claims.title: Type Five virtue: detachment
claims.content: The virtue of Enneagram Type Five is detachment, also called nonattachment.

claims.title: Envy arises from losing equanimity
claims.content: Envy results from losing contact with the virtue of equanimity and leads people to feel that something is missing in them.

claims.title: Avarice is not only materialism
claims.content: Avarice does not necessarily express itself through materialistic greed or the accumulation of possessions.

claims.title: Equanimity: emotional balance
claims.content: Equanimity means emotional balance, the virtue that corresponds to the Enneagram Type Four passion of envy.

claims.title: Type Five fixation: stinginess
claims.content: The fixation of Enneagram Type Five is stinginess.

claims.title: Holy Origin: direct experience of Essence
claims.content: Holy Origin is the direct experience of one's true identity as Essence, with Being as its source, rather than a concept or belief.

claims.title: Type Five holy ideas
claims.content: The holy ideas of Enneagram Type Five are Holy Omniscience and Holy Transparency.

claims.title: Envy drives self-comparison with others
claims.content: In envy, people compare themselves with others and believe others have qualities, luck, or childhoods they lack.

claims.title: Nonattachment term choice
claims.content: The authors use nonattachment instead of Ichazo's original term Detachment to distinguish it from emotional withdrawal.

claims.title: Type Six holy idea
claims.content: Holy Faith is the holy idea of Type Six.

claims.title: Type Six virtue courage
claims.content: Courage is the virtue of Type Six.

claims.title: Fear as Type Six passion
claims.content: Fear, the passion of Type Six, is the feeling that arises when a person feels unsupported and without guidance.

claims.title: Type Six four traits
claims.content: Type Six has the passion fear, the virtue courage, the fixation cowardice, and the holy idea Holy Faith.

claims.title: Avarice confused with Gluttony
claims.content: Avarice is often confused with Gluttony, the passion of Type Seven.

claims.title: Avarice as collecting knowledge
claims.content: Avarice in Type Five often appears as a collector mentality, gathering more knowledge and preparing before going out into the world.

claims.title: Avarice as Type Five passion
claims.content: Avarice, the passion of Type Five, leads Fives to feel rejected by the universe and to retreat from or defend against reality.

claims.title: Nonattachment as Type Five virtue
claims.content: Nonattachment, the virtue of Type Five, means not clinging to anything inner or outer and requires radical acceptance of reality.

claims.title: Type Five stinginess effects
claims.content: Fives who believe they need more information or skill before living find it hard to start their lives and to give generously.

claims.title: Stinginess as Type Five fixation
claims.content: Stinginess, the fixation of Type Five, is the ego mind's tendency to hold on to experiences and information to build knowledge and power.

claims.title: Holy Omniscience as Type Five idea
claims.content: Holy Omniscience, the holy idea of Type Five, is a direct apprehension of the knowing-ness of Essence.

claims.title: Type Six fixation cowardice
claims.content: Cowardice is the fixation of Type Six.

claims.title: Holy Faith as recognized support
claims.content: Holy Faith is the recognition that the actual support of presence and Being is available now, and that Essence is real and cannot be lost; it is not a belief.

claims.title: Sevens pursue excess experiences
claims.content: Sevens believe they can fill inner emptiness with exciting experiences and often fail to distinguish wants from needs, pursuing excess in every area of life.

claims.title: Cowardice as Type Six fixation
claims.content: Cowardice is the Fixation of Type Six, meaning a failure of confidence in one's ability to know and receive inner guidance, also called doubt.

claims.title: Type Six anxiety from lacking guidance
claims.content: Type Six lacks contact with inner guidance, which leaves Sixes anxious and unsure how to decide, avoid danger, and move forward.

claims.title: Gluttony as Type Seven passion
claims.content: Gluttony, the Passion of Type Seven, is the belief that all good and desirable things exist outside oneself and must be obtained, arising from an inner emptiness the ego tries to suppress.

claims.title: Sevens' external filling backfires
claims.content: The more Sevens try to fill themselves with things and experiences, the less able they become to find the fulfillment they seek.

claims.title: Courage as Enneagram virtue
claims.content: Courage is the Virtue of Type Six, meaning the absence of fear, which differs from defying fear or aggressively toughening oneself up (counterphobia).

claims.title: Type Six fears often hypothetical
claims.content: Type Six fears are often based on things that might happen rather than on current reality.

claims.title: Holy Faith gives inner freedom
claims.content: Holy Faith gives an unshakable confidence in the inherent goodness of life and lets a person respond spontaneously without being bound by beliefs, doubts, or learned procedures.

claims.title: Type Six hedging and self-doubt
claims.content: Sixes try to hedge against life by seeking stability and social security, and their cowardice leads them to second-guess and doubt their own decisions.

claims.title: Type Seven trait summary
claims.content: Type Seven has the Passion of gluttony, the Virtue of sobriety, the Fixation of planning, and the Holy Ideas of Holy Wisdom, Holy Work, and Holy Plan.

claims.title: Type Six control does not reduce fear
claims.content: Type Six organizes and systematizes its environment to make it predictable, but this activity does not reduce its fear.

claims.title: Type Seven fixation: planning
claims.content: The fixation of Type Seven is planning, which fills the mind with exciting future projects and tries to make future experiences optimal.

claims.title: Type Eight passion: lust
claims.content: The passion of Type Eight is lust, which the source describes as an addiction to intensity rather than primarily sexual lust.

claims.title: Type Seven holy idea: Holy Wisdom
claims.content: The holy idea of Type Seven includes Holy Wisdom, which recognizes that the Divine Plan is unfolding perfectly in the present moment.

claims.title: Type Eight fixation: vengeance
claims.content: The fixation of Type Eight is vengeance.

claims.title: Type Seven virtue: sobriety
claims.content: The virtue of Type Seven is sobriety, a grounded and clear awareness of the present moment.

claims.title: Type Eight virtue: innocence
claims.content: The virtue of Type Eight is innocence, which involves behaving without artifice or manipulation and responding to life with sincere, direct, heartfelt responses.

claims.title: Type Eight holy idea: Holy Truth
claims.content: The holy idea of Type Eight is Holy Truth.

claims.title: Holy Work: conscious participation
claims.content: Holy Work is consciously participating in the miraculous unfolding of reality, which the source describes as the greatest source of satisfaction.

claims.title: Fixated justice as retribution
claims.content: From the fixated perspective, Eights' sense of justice often means retribution.

claims.title: Type Nine attributes
claims.content: Type Nine has the Passion of Sloth, the Virtue of Action, the Fixation of Indolence, and the Holy Idea of Holy Love.

claims.title: Eights' reaction to loss
claims.content: Eights react to the loss of Holy Truth by feeling that someone must be responsible, feeling rejected and angry.

claims.title: Holy Truth: All is One
claims.content: The Holy Truth is that All is One: there is only one reality, and all levels and manifestations of existence are part of it.

claims.title: Fixated Eights see struggle
claims.content: Eights caught in the Fixation of Vengeance tend to see everything as a struggle to be overcome.

claims.title: Eight Fixation: Vengeance
claims.content: The Fixation of Eights is Vengeance, the ego's response to the loss of Holy Truth.

claims.title: Holy Truth ends separateness
claims.content: Perceiving Holy Truth ends the sense of separateness, alienation, fear, and desire.

claims.title: Holy Love: dynamic force
claims.content: Holy Love is a living, dynamic force that dissolves barriers and boundaries and restores awareness to unity with Truth.

claims.title: Holy Love: recognition of oneness
claims.content: Holy Love is the recognition that all is one and that this oneness is ultimately benevolent and supportive.

claims.title: Type One traits overview
claims.content: Enneagram Type One has the Passion of anger (resentment), the Virtue of serenity, the Fixation of resentment and judging, and the Holy Idea of Holy Perfection.

claims.title: Indolence: presence without content
claims.content: Indolence leads people to be present without content, and as it deepens, they lose meaningful awareness of others.

claims.title: Anger: resistance becomes resentment
claims.content: When people are not present to their anger, they resist its natural unfolding and develop tension, frustration, and resentment that becomes a constant underlying feeling.

claims.title: Nines: imagined peace defended
claims.content: Nines create an imitation of wholeness and benevolence in their imaginations and defend that inner peace against the dynamic processes of reality.

claims.title: Nines: surface versus depth
claims.content: Nines seem easygoing, agreeable, and adaptable on the surface, but at a deeper level they do not want to be made to change.

claims.title: Serenity: accepting reality
claims.content: Serenity is accepting reality as it is when awake and present, without feeling separate from others or better or worse than them.

claims.title: Serenity: self-acceptance
claims.content: Serenity includes accepting oneself, one's body, and one's feelings, and allowing life's energies to flow without resisting or controlling them.

claims.title: Ones: self-image under control
claims.content: Ones usually see themselves as 'under control' and as always striving to get things right, not as angry.

claims.title: Passion of anger: origin
claims.content: The Passion of anger is the Passion of Type One, and it results from the loss of the Virtue of Serenity.

claims.title: Holy Love: trust in Being
claims.content: Knowing Holy Love leads people to relax ego activity and trust Being to support them.

claims.title: Indolence: avoids suffering
claims.content: Indolence leads people to disengage attention from their core self to avoid feeling the suffering of lost contact with Holy Love.

claims.title: Ones: unaware of resentment
claims.content: Ones fully resist expressing their anger and are often unaware of it as a constant backdrop of smoldering resentment.

claims.title: Indolence: attention avoids interior
claims.content: Indolence is an ego fixation in which attention avoids deep contact with one's interior being.

claims.title: Type One virtue: serenity
claims.content: The Virtue of Serenity is the Virtue of Type One.

claims.title: Ones: suppressed anger expressed
claims.content: Suppressed anger in Ones is eventually expressed, often inappropriately, with negative consequences for their relationships.

claims.title: Type One holy idea: Holy Perfection
claims.content: The Holy Idea of Holy Perfection is the Holy Idea of Type One.

claims.title: Anger: chronic dissatisfaction
claims.content: The Passion of anger causes chronic dissatisfaction with oneself and with reality, leading people to feel that reality is not the way it ought to be.

claims.title: Indolence perpetuates Sloth
claims.content: Indolence serves to perpetuate Sloth in Nines.

claims.title: Nines: dissociation under threat
claims.content: Nines use dissociation, mentally checking out when situations threaten to uncover their loss of contact with Holy Love.

claims.title: Type One fixation: resentment, judging
claims.content: The Fixation of resentment and judging is the Fixation of Type One.

claims.title: Serenity: no striving
claims.content: In serenity there is no feeling of effort or striving, and a person feels calm and balanced through life's ups and downs.

claims.title: Anger: natural unfolding
claims.content: Anger arises spontaneously when someone or something threatens a person's integrity, lasts a few moments, and then passes.

claims.title: Type One fixation: resentment and judging
claims.content: The Fixation of Enneagram Type One is resentment and judging.

claims.title: Holy Perfection defined
claims.content: Holy Perfection is the Holy Idea in which a fully present person experiences reality as unfolding perfectly according to a Divine Plan.

claims.title: Holy Perfection does not excuse inaction
claims.content: Holy Perfection does not mean ignoring suffering or refusing to help when help is possible.

claims.title: Type One seeks lost perfection
claims.content: Enneagram Type One's ego tries to recreate a sense of perfection that is part of its Essence.

claims.title: Type One resentment from lost perfection
claims.content: Enneagram Type One's resentment results from losing the sense of Holy Perfection.

claims.title: Security Point behavior limits
claims.content: The Security Point describes behaviors from the average range of a type's Direction of Integration, shown only with people the person feels secure with.

claims.title: Judging divides the self
claims.content: The ego activity of judging divides the self into judging and judged parts, which destroys the unity of the self.

claims.title: Perfection requires whole-self contact
claims.content: Embodying and recognizing perfection requires whole and complete contact with all of the self.

claims.title: Type One striving sustains anger
claims.content: Enneagram Type One believes aspects of itself and the world are flawed, and its anger about apparent imperfection sustains its passion.

claims.title: Childhood memory distortion
claims.content: Childhood memories may be distorted, so a person may not know their true relationship with their parents.

claims.title: Seven childhood pattern with mother
claims.content: Sevens are disconnected from and frustrated with their nurturer or mother figure, and this early difficulty can remain imprinted even after later friendship with the mother.

claims.title: Fathering and mothering functions
claims.content: The fathering functions provide guidance, protection, structure, and support for coping with the outer world, while the mothering functions provide nurturing, mirroring, a sense of value and identity.

claims.title: Seven denial and childhood troubles
claims.content: Denial, a defense mechanism often present in average to unhealthy Sevens, can make it difficult for them to face childhood troubles, often until years of therapy reveal the true picture.

claims.title: Childhood Patterns origin in threes
claims.content: The Enneagram Childhood Patterns were developed by Don Riso from three groups of three, yielding nine combinations matched to the nine Enneagram types.

claims.title: Childhood Pattern refinements
claims.content: The Childhood Patterns framework was refined by recognizing that patterns form in the first three years of life and that the relationship is with the category of experience a parent represents, not only a specific person.

claims.title: Holding environment term
claims.content: Modern psychology uses the term holding environment for the whole quality of childhood environment that includes both fathering and mothering functions.

claims.title: Childhood Patterns do not cause type
claims.content: The authors state that the prenatal and genetic basis for personality, called temperament, is likely the primary determinant of personality type, so Childhood Patterns do not cause type.

claims.title: Childhood Pattern relationship categories
claims.content: The Childhood Patterns framework groups early parent-child relationships as connected, disconnected, or ambivalent, with each group relating a child to mother, father, or both parents.

claims.title: Childhood Patterns evidence limits
claims.content: The authors state that the Childhood Patterns are anecdotal and have not been formally researched, though they may give researchers hypotheses to test.

claims.title: Orientation and parenting responses
claims.content: Types with a connected orientation attach strongly to the parenting function in question, disconnected types feel frustrated with it, and ambivalent types feel rejected by the parent.

claims.title: Childhood Patterns not for typing alone
claims.content: The authors do not recommend determining personality type by using the Childhood Patterns alone, because they are one factor among many and should not be given undue weight.

claims.title: Characteristic Temptation as warning signal
claims.content: A Characteristic Temptation can act as an early warning signal of more neurotic behavior, while there is still time to avoid it.

claims.title: At least three defenses per type
claims.content: Each Enneagram type has at least three key Defense Mechanisms, and probably more, according to the authors' investigations.

claims.title: Basic Fear and Basic Desire
claims.content: Basic Fear and Basic Desire are unconscious motivations, arising from childhood responses to the parents' holding environment, that underlie ordinary conscious motivations.

claims.title: Basic Fear glossary entry
claims.content: PPE-style glossary note: Basic Fear is the unconscious fear that underlies a type's motivations, as described in the source.

claims.title: Hidden Complaint defined
claims.content: The Hidden Complaint is an unstated, frustrated claim made about the self that becomes more prominent as a person declines toward fixation and unhealth.

claims.title: Basic Fear and Basic Desire by type
claims.content: Basic Fear and Basic Desire are unique to each Enneagram personality type and produce that type's secondary fears, desires, and traits at each Level of Development.

claims.title: Healthy sense of self defined
claims.content: A healthy sense of self is a stable, unconscious goal that arises from each type's Basic Fear, Basic Desire, cognitive functions, and defense mechanisms.

claims.title: Sense of self shifts by level
claims.content: A person's sense of self shifts as they move up or down the Levels of Development.

claims.title: Characteristic Temptation defined
claims.content: A Characteristic Temptation is a way of thinking or behaving that begins a type's fixation, typically at Level 4.

claims.title: Secondary Motivations defined
claims.content: Secondary Motivations are the derivative fears and desires that arise from each type's Basic Fear and Basic Desire at each Level of Development.

claims.title: Motivations needed to tell types apart
claims.content: Traits alone do not reveal an Enneagram type, so the motivations underlying observed traits must be understood to tell types apart.

claims.title: Hidden Complaint and interpersonal conflict
claims.content: The Hidden Complaint is the unacknowledged source of many of a type's interpersonal conflicts and underlying attitudes toward others.

claims.title: Defense Mechanisms explain type patterns
claims.content: Defense Mechanisms explain each type's motivation, behavior, and how it defends its sense of self, and they produce different patterns for each type.

claims.title: Traditional single defense per type
claims.content: The traditional Enneagram teaching lists one defense mechanism per type, attributed to Claudio Naranjo.

claims.title: Unrealistic sense of self causes anxiety
claims.content: An unrealistic sense of self, whether inflated or too negative, causes anxiety that triggers defense mechanisms.

claims.title: Saving Grace enables reversal
claims.content: A Saving Grace can prevent a deteriorating person from sliding further and can help restore healthier functioning only if the person is aware of it and able to act on it.

claims.title: Saving Grace defined
claims.content: The Saving Grace is the remaining positive quality that persists in a person who has deteriorated to Level 6 and can be drawn on to help that person recover.

claims.title: Type Two integration toward Four
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's direction of integration is toward Type Four, where healthy Twos become emotionally honest and accept their full range of feelings.

claims.title: Type Two basic desire
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's basic desire is to feel loved.

claims.title: Type Two hidden complaint
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's hidden complaint is that they are always loving but people do not love them as much as they love others, and that they are taken for granted and unappreciated.

claims.title: Type Two defense mechanisms
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's key defense mechanisms are identification, reaction formation, and denial.

claims.title: Type Two search for intimacy
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's search for intimacy seeks a relationship in which they are truly welcomed, close, and deeply wanted.

claims.title: Type Two indirect expression of needs
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's structural pattern is indirection: personal needs are expressed indirectly through service to others.

claims.title: Type Two basic fear
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two, the Two, has a basic fear of being unloved and unwanted for themselves alone.

claims.title: Type Two characteristic temptation
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's characteristic temptation is to believe they are without needs and always well intentioned.

claims.title: Type Two childhood pattern
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's childhood pattern involves learning to win love by serving or pleasing others, often while feeling rejected by the household's guiding authority figure, often the father.

claims.title: Type Two healthy self-sense
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's healthy self-sense is "I am a caring, loving person."

claims.title: Type Two disintegration toward Eight
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's direction of disintegration is toward Type Eight, where average Twos suddenly assert their needs more forcefully under failure or increased stress.

claims.title: Type Two stress dependency control
claims.content: Under extreme stress, unhealthy Enneagram Twos may attempt to control others by creating dependencies.

claims.title: Twos' controlling behavior repels
claims.content: The more intrusive, manipulative, coercive, or domineering less healthy Twos become, the more they drive others away.

claims.title: Twos' value depends on others
claims.content: Less healthy Twos believe their value depends on others responding to them in specific ways.

claims.title: Twos need honesty about needs
claims.content: Twos can realize their desire to be loving and supportive only if they are honest about their own needs and limitations.

claims.title: Twos balance others' and own needs
claims.content: Twos need to balance their focus on others' needs with an honest acknowledgment of their own needs.

claims.title: Twos' desire and fear reinforce
claims.content: As less healthy Twos deteriorate, they undermine their Basic Desire to be loved and increasingly bring on their Basic Fear of being unloved.

claims.title: Average Threes driven to excel
claims.content: Average Enneagram Threes become driven to excel, so that nearly all their activities serve their bid for success.

claims.title: Average Threes compare themselves
claims.content: Average Threes can become anxious comparing themselves and their achievements with others.

claims.title: Rejection raises Twos' expectations
claims.content: The more rejected Twos feel, the greater their expectation for a loving response from others.

claims.title: Twos signal wants indirectly
claims.content: Less healthy Enneagram Twos communicate what they want from others indirectly, through hints, without saying so openly.

claims.title: Average Threes seek recognition
claims.content: Average Threes focus on their performance, seek recognition for accomplishments, and need to be the best at whatever they do.

claims.title: Healthy Threes' ambition
claims.content: Healthy Threes are ambitious to improve themselves and often become outstanding in some way, embodying widely admired qualities.

claims.title: Basic Desire defined
claims.content: Basic Desire is a personality type's core desire; for Enneagram Type Two it is to be loved.

claims.title: Healthy Threes' self-assurance
claims.content: Healthy Enneagram Threes are self-assured, feel desirable, and have high self-esteem.

claims.title: Twos' conflict causes suffering
claims.content: Repressed conflicts in unhealthy Twos often produce conscious suffering and physical ailments.

claims.title: Twos' hidden reward expectation
claims.content: For Twos, the problem is not their generosity but the hidden expectation that it will be rewarded with appreciation and reciprocal caring.

claims.title: Healthy Threes meet challenges
claims.content: Healthy Threes meet challenges by being highly competent, focused, diligent, and extremely adaptable.

claims.title: Twos' hidden needs cause conflict
claims.content: Unacknowledged needs and covert claims cause conflict between unhealthy Twos' loving feelings and their unconscious resentments.

claims.title: Twos need self-nurturing
claims.content: Twos need to nurture themselves as well as they would like to nurture others.

claims.title: Less healthy Threes' image focus
claims.content: Less healthy Threes become highly image-conscious and concerned with projecting an acceptable image.

claims.title: Threes fear being seen through
claims.content: Less healthy Threes fear that others will see through them, so problems with commitment and intimacy emerge.

claims.title: Threes inflate their talents
claims.content: Less healthy Threes feel compelled to impress others with their achievements and inflate their talents.

claims.title: Twos' conflict shows as coercion
claims.content: Unhealthy Twos express inner conflict as overbearing, coercive behavior toward others and as self-sacrifice and moral masochism toward themselves.

claims.title: Conflict signals Two's self-deception
claims.content: Consistent interpersonal conflict is a strong indication that a Two is falling into prideful self-deception.

claims.title: Basic Fear defined
claims.content: Basic Fear is a personality type's core fear; for Enneagram Type Two it is that they are unloved and unwanted for themselves alone.

claims.title: Healthy Threes accept themselves
claims.content: At their best, healthy Threes accept themselves and do not feel they must become more successful to be worthwhile.

claims.title: Twos' praise-seeking backfires
claims.content: When Twos call attention to themselves or expect praise for what they give, they move in the wrong direction and become frustrated.

claims.title: Feeling Triad definition
claims.content: Feeling Triad is a grouping of three types that the source describes as feeling-centered; Enneagram Type Three is its primary type.

claims.title: Direction of Disintegration definition
claims.content: Direction of Disintegration is the type whose average behaviors a type acts out under excessive stress; for Enneagram Type Three, it is Type Nine.

claims.title: Unhealthy Threes deny problems
claims.content: Unhealthy Enneagram Type Threes become desperate to appear superior and deny their emotional problems, which often leads to burnout and chronic depression.

claims.title: Basic Fear definition
claims.content: Basic Fear is the core fear that a type holds about itself, which drives its patterns; for Enneagram Type Three, it is being worthless.

claims.title: Threes act out Six behaviors
claims.content: Average Enneagram Type Threes sometimes act out average Type Six behaviors, usually with trusted friends and intimates, revealing their self-doubt, pessimism, and anxiety.

claims.title: Threes' childhood origin
claims.content: Enneagram Type Threes often learned as children that they were loved mainly for their performance, so they adapted to please a nurturing figure, often the mother, and became the family hero.

claims.title: Stress moves Threes toward Nine
claims.content: When average Enneagram Type Threes push themselves beyond their limit, stress can make them act out average Type Nine behaviors, leaving them disengaged, running on autopilot, and vague.

claims.title: Threes suppress real feelings
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three is the most out of touch with its own real feelings in the Feeling Triad, and its hurt and shame are suppressed to meet the expectations of significant others.

claims.title: Threes' basic fear
claims.content: The basic fear of Enneagram Type Three is being worthless.

claims.title: Unhealthy Threes turn dishonest
claims.content: If unhealthy Enneagram Type Threes do not seek help, they may become dishonest, for example by submitting false résumés or committing plagiarism.

claims.title: Basic Desire definition
claims.content: Basic Desire is the core desire that a type seeks to satisfy; for Enneagram Type Three, it is to feel valuable.

claims.title: Healthy Threes move toward Six
claims.content: Healthy Enneagram Type Threes who move toward Type Six become committed to others, cooperative rather than competitive, and find deep satisfaction in working with others.

claims.title: Direction of Integration definition
claims.content: Direction of Integration is the type a healthy person moves toward to grow; for Enneagram Type Three, it is Type Six.

claims.title: Security Point definition
claims.content: Security Point is the type whose average behaviors a type sometimes acts out with trusted people; for Enneagram Type Three, the Security Point is Type Six.

claims.title: Extreme unhealthy Three behavior
claims.content: In extreme cases, deeply unhealthy Enneagram Type Threes may maliciously betray or sabotage people and show psychopathic tendencies.

claims.title: Unrelieved stress in Threes
claims.content: If their stress is not relieved, unhealthy Enneagram Type Threes become passive, resigned, and depressed, and under severe stress they may dissociate from their feelings.

claims.title: Threes' basic desire
claims.content: The basic desire of Enneagram Type Three is to feel valuable.

claims.title: Type Three cognitive error
claims.content: Threes' cognitive error is thinking that their value comes from their performance or external image, such as success in wealth, social standing, or professional accomplishment.

claims.title: Ego self lacks inherent value
claims.content: The ego self is inherently without value, and it requires constant attention and outer support to maintain its sense of importance.

claims.title: Type Three acceptance guides balance
claims.content: Threes' healthy desire to be accepted by others may guide them away from competitions and back to balanced behavior.

claims.title: Type Three seeks external validation
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people seek acceptance and validation from others because they are typically blocked from experiencing their Essential quality of Personal Value.

claims.title: Type Three detachment from Essence
claims.content: Threes remain detached from their Essence, the only real source of value and identity, regardless of their success or admiration.

claims.title: Authenticity sustains Type Three admiration
claims.content: Threes who want to enjoy others' admiration must remain authentic.

claims.title: Unhealthy Threes hidden dependence
claims.content: Average to unhealthy Threes are covertly dependent on others' acceptance beneath a highly functional, independent facade.

claims.title: Type Three defense mechanisms
claims.content: Type Three's key defense mechanisms are repression, projection, and displacement.

claims.title: Type Four aesthetic expression
claims.content: Healthy Type Fours emphasize beauty and enjoy expressing their feelings aesthetically.

claims.title: Lower road for Threes
claims.content: Without a heart connection, Threes may gain fleeting fame or recognition but remain untouched by it, and the lower road leads to loneliness, empty victories, and emotional disconnection.

claims.title: Type Three saving grace
claims.content: Average Threes' desire to feel valuable and worthwhile may prevent them from engaging in deceptive or dishonest activities that could cause shame and humiliation.

claims.title: Healthy Type Four solitude
claims.content: Healthy Type Fours enjoy being alone and take time for their unconscious impulses to surface into consciousness.

claims.title: Type Three structural keynote
claims.content: The keynote of Enneagram Type Three's structural pattern is adaptability.

claims.title: Average Threes drive for success
claims.content: Average Threes can become caught up in a relentless drive for success and a need to demonstrate their superiority to others.

claims.title: Authenticity grants Type Three desire
claims.content: Authenticity gives Threes their Basic Desire, because people value and esteem those who embody presence and heart connection.

claims.title: Ego inflation undermines Type Three desire
claims.content: Ego inflation causes Threes to undermine their Basic Desire to feel valuable and worthwhile while bringing on their Basic Fear of feeling worthless.

claims.title: Healthy Type Four self-expression
claims.content: Healthy Type Fours are self-expressive, highly personal, individualistic, and emotionally honest.

claims.title: Type Three basic fear of worthlessness
claims.content: Type Three's Basic Fear is of being worthless, and Threes seek a steady supply of admiring attention to counteract it.

claims.title: Type Three adaptive identity formation
claims.content: Threes form their identities and interact with others by adapting to people, responding to others' expectations, and adjusting to the feedback they receive.

claims.title: Type Four Individualist description
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four, the Individualist, is described as expressive, dramatic, self-absorbed, and temperamental.

claims.title: Type Three hidden complaint
claims.content: Type Three's hidden complaint is "I am a superior person, but other people are jealous of me."

claims.title: Authenticity defined as presence
claims.content: Authenticity means being present, connected deeply with one's heart, and acting from that presence and connection.

claims.title: Healthy Type Four traits
claims.content: Healthy Type Fours are introspective, self-aware, in touch with feelings and inner impulses, and in search of self.

claims.title: Type Three temptation to be best
claims.content: Average Threes have a characteristic temptation to constantly push themselves to be "the best."

claims.title: Type Three healthy sense of self
claims.content: Type Three's healthy sense of self is "I am an outstanding, effective person."

claims.title: Type Four at their best
claims.content: At their best, Type Fours are profoundly creative, expressing the personal and the universal, possibly in an inspired work of art.

claims.title: Average Threes inner emptiness
claims.content: The inner pattern of average Threes is emotional vulnerability or emptiness, concealed by a superb capacity for social interaction and adaptability.

claims.title: Healthy Type Four interpersonal traits
claims.content: Healthy Type Fours are sensitive and intuitive toward self and others, and are compassionate, tactful, discreet, and respectful of others.

claims.title: Healthy Type Four openness to feeling
claims.content: Healthy Type Fours are passionate about relationships and inner lives, willing to explore any feeling without judging it.

claims.title: Four's personal, outsider feelings
claims.content: Average Fours interiorize everything and take it personally, often feeling they are different or outsiders.

claims.title: Direction of Disintegration defined
claims.content: Direction of Disintegration is the path a type takes under stress, and for Enneagram Type Four it leads toward Type Two.

claims.title: Healthy Four's move toward One
claims.content: Healthy Fours who move toward One act on objective principles and are self-disciplined rather than self-indulgent.

claims.title: Four's withdrawal to protect self-image
claims.content: Average Fours may withdraw to protect their self-image and to sort out their feelings.

claims.title: Extreme breakdown risks in Fours
claims.content: In the extreme, emotional breakdown in unhealthy Fours is likely to lead to crimes of passion or suicide.

claims.title: Four's hostility expression
claims.content: Fours express hostility through envy, rancorous sarcasm, and cutting off connections when their identity is questioned or threatened.

claims.title: Direction of Integration defined
claims.content: Direction of Integration is the path a type takes when healthy, and for Enneagram Type Four it leads toward Type One.

claims.title: Unhealthy Four's temperament and hostility
claims.content: Unhealthy Fours become temperamental and hostile to anyone who questions their lifestyle.

claims.title: Four's artistic romantic orientation
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four moves toward an artistic, romantic orientation that cultivates a beautiful, aesthetic environment and personal feelings.

claims.title: Four's One behaviors with intimates
claims.content: Average Fours can act out average behaviors of Type One, usually with trusted friends and intimates, including a superior attitude and perfectionism.

claims.title: Blocked Feeling Center in Fours
claims.content: A blocked Feeling Center leads Fours to use their imagination to stimulate and prolong the emotional reactions on which they base their sense of self.

claims.title: Unhealthy Four's rejection and dependence
claims.content: Unhealthy Fours reject anyone or anything that does not support their self-image and become increasingly dependent on a few people.

claims.title: Security Point defined
claims.content: Security Point is the type whose average behaviors a type can adopt with trusted friends and intimates, and for Enneagram Type Four it is Type One.

claims.title: Stress shifts Fours toward Two
claims.content: Stress can cause average Fours, especially in significant relationships, to take on the behaviors of average Twos, such as people-pleasing.

claims.title: Four's triad identity and hostility issues
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four shares issues with identity and hostility with the other types in its triad.

claims.title: Type Four grounding in reality
claims.content: Enneagram Type Fours find themselves by grounding themselves in the realities of the here and now.

claims.title: Saving Grace (Type Four)
claims.content: Saving Grace is the quality that may keep a type from further decline; for average Enneagram Type Fours, it is self-awareness and honesty with themselves.

claims.title: Basic Fear (Type Four)
claims.content: Basic Fear is the core fear a type holds; for Enneagram Type Four, it is the fear of having no identity or personal significance.

claims.title: Type Four inward spiral
claims.content: As Enneagram Type Fours deteriorate, they spiral inward into self-enclosed negative states and may become alienated from others and themselves if they cannot break the pattern of introversion.

claims.title: Hidden Complaint (Type Four)
claims.content: Hidden Complaint is the unspoken grievance a type holds; for Enneagram Type Four, it is feeling different from others and not fitting in.

claims.title: Type Four subjectivity keynote
claims.content: The structural keynote of Enneagram Type Fours is subjectivity, so they personalize experience and often assign meaning where none exists.

claims.title: Type Four relationship frustrations
claims.content: Enneagram Type Fours may recreate frustrations from childhood, when they felt abandoned or misunderstood by their parents, in their adult relationships and take out dissatisfaction on key intimates.

claims.title: Characteristic Temptation (Type Four)
claims.content: Characteristic Temptation is the habit a type is most drawn to; for Enneagram Type Four, it is overusing the imagination in the search for self.

claims.title: Type Four ego inflation effects
claims.content: For Enneagram Type Fours, ego inflation in fantasies and subjective withdrawal undermines their Basic Desire and increases their Basic Fear.

claims.title: Key Defense Mechanisms (Type Four)
claims.content: Key Defense Mechanisms are the habitual defenses a type relies on; for Enneagram Type Four, they are introjection, displacement, splitting, and turning against the self.

claims.title: Healthy Sense of Self (Type Four)
claims.content: Healthy Sense of Self is the self-description a type holds when healthy; for Enneagram Type Four, it is "I am an intuitive, sensitive person."

claims.title: Type Four fantasy retreat
claims.content: Average to unhealthy Enneagram Type Fours retreat into fantasies, losing themselves in imagination instead of dealing with reality.

claims.title: Cognitive Error (Type Four)
claims.content: Cognitive Error is the thinking mistake a type tends to make; for Enneagram Type Four, it is identifying with changing feelings and emotional states, especially negative ones.

claims.title: Basic Desire (Type Four)
claims.content: Basic Desire is the core want a type pursues; for Enneagram Type Four, it is to be themselves.

claims.title: Type Five growth direction to Eight
claims.content: Healthy Enneagram Type Fives move toward Type Eight, becoming grounded in their bodies and acting with confidence from their own mastery.

claims.title: Type Five unhealthy traits
claims.content: Unhealthy Enneagram Type Fives become reclusive, isolated, and suspicious, and severe depression and nihilism are common.

claims.title: Type Five Thinking Center identity
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five is identified with the Thinking Center, and its overactive mind leaves little connection with the physical body.

claims.title: Type Five average tendencies
claims.content: Average Enneagram Type Fives retreat into their inner world of concepts and imagination and become detached from practical life.

claims.title: Type Five stress direction to Seven
claims.content: Under stress, Enneagram Type Fives move toward the average behaviors of Type Seven, becoming scattered, impulsive, and compulsive.

claims.title: Type Five anxiety and retreat
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five's anxiety about the outside world leads it to retreat into the mind, which it sees as safer and more secure.

claims.title: Type Five severe unhealthy outcomes
claims.content: Under severe unhealthy conditions, Enneagram Type Fives may experience psychotic breaks or commit suicide, according to the file.

claims.title: Type Five healthy traits
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five, the Investigator, is perceptive, curious, and innovative, and often becomes an expert in a field.

claims.title: Type Five mastery activities
claims.content: Average to unhealthy Enneagram Type Five individuals may master subjects such as math, piano, chess, or computer games to gain confidence and avoid intrusion into their private space.

claims.title: Type Five childhood overwhelm
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five individuals, as children, often feel overwhelmed by their caretakers' needs and uncertain what they can contribute to the family.

claims.title: Type Five projection under strain
claims.content: When subjective impulses overpower Enneagram Type Five perception, Fives unconsciously project subjective ideas onto their perceptions.

claims.title: Type Five temptation to conceptualize
claims.content: The characteristic temptation of Enneagram Type Five individuals is to replace direct experience with concepts.

claims.title: Type Five mastery goal
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five individuals seek mastery of something to feel more confident and ready to meet life's challenges.

claims.title: Type Five basic desire
claims.content: The basic desire of Enneagram Type Five individuals is to be capable and competent, to be able to do.

claims.title: Type Five influence on observation
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five individuals participate in the world and affect the subjects they observe, regardless of whether they like it.

claims.title: Type Five outside observer error
