claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven individuals are driven by anxiety, while Enneagram Type One individuals are driven by simmering anger.

claims.title: Ones moralize and scold others
claims.content: Enneagram Type One individuals moralize and scold others, lecturing them in the name of an ideal about issues they care about.

claims.title: Sixes rely on reassurance and procedure
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six individuals are uncertain and rely on reassurance, back-up, familiar procedure, or previously tested ideas to help them make decisions.

claims.title: Low-functioning Ones rarely violent
claims.content: Lower functioning Enneagram Type One individuals can be sarcastic and verbally abusive but almost never lose control and are seldom physically violent.

claims.title: Sixes aware of anxious tension
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six individuals carry considerable anxious tension and are more aware of that tension.

claims.title: Ones and Sixes: should and must
claims.content: Enneagram Types One and Six are both 'should' and 'must' people who feel obligated to complete all duties before relaxing or attending to their own needs.

claims.title: Named examples of Ones and Sevens
claims.content: George F. Will and Julie Andrews are cited as Enneagram Type One examples, and Larry King and Cameron Diaz as Type Seven examples.

claims.title: Sixes' main negative feelings
claims.content: The principal negative feelings in Enneagram Type Six individuals are fearfulness, suspicion, and anxiety.

claims.title: Ones' main negative emotions
claims.content: The principal negative emotions in Enneagram Type One individuals are righteous anger, irritation, and moral indignation.

claims.title: Low-functioning Sixes lose tempers
claims.content: Low functioning Enneagram Type Six individuals can more easily lose their tempers, sometimes erupting into hysterical reactions or even physical violence.

claims.title: Bush and Gore as type examples
claims.content: George Bush and Al Gore are cited as examples of Enneagram Type Six and Type One, respectively.

claims.title: Ones expect disappointment
claims.content: Enneagram Type One individuals hold high standards and expect to be disappointed by people and by the world.

claims.title: Sixes aggressive toward rejecters
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six individuals can be aggressive toward anyone who does not share their values, especially when they are more insecure.

claims.title: Average Sixes struggle with volatile feelings
claims.content: Average Enneagram Type Six individuals struggle with more volatile feelings and have difficulty putting them aside, although they seldom express those feelings to others.

claims.title: Sevens mistake frustration for perfectionism
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven individuals mistake their frustration or impatience with the quality of their experience for perfectionism.

claims.title: Ones berate themselves over errors
claims.content: Enneagram Type One individuals berate themselves for days over small errors, such as a misplaced comma in an otherwise excellent report.

claims.title: One justice as principle
claims.content: Enneagram Type One holds justice as a matter of principle and seeks to rectify injustices to meet its high moral standards and avoid guilt.

claims.title: One and Eight self-misidentification
claims.content: Some Enneagram Type Ones may misidentify themselves as Type Eight, but Type Eights almost never misidentify themselves as Type One.

claims.title: One persuasion style
claims.content: Enneagram Type One tries to persuade others from a moral imperative and logic, and becomes irritated when others resist its reasoning.

claims.title: Unhealthy One and Eight justice
claims.content: Unhealthy Enneagram Type One rationalizes punitive actions as fair, while unhealthy Enneagram Type Eight administers justice as vengeance.

claims.title: Instinctive Triad grouping
claims.content: The Instinctive Triad is a grouping of Enneagram types that includes Type One and Type Eight.

claims.title: One and Nine confusion source
claims.content: Ones and Nines are often confused when it is unclear whether the wing or the dominant type is which.

claims.title: One justice as reward and punishment
claims.content: Enneagram Type One seeks to ensure people are rewarded for good actions and punished for bad ones.

claims.title: One drive and anxiety
claims.content: Enneagram Type One is extremely driven, struggles to rest, and feels anxious when not being productive.

claims.title: Eight justice targets power imbalance
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight's sense of justice usually addresses an imbalance of power.

claims.title: Eight persuasion style
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight relies on self-confidence, gutsy convictions, and personal charisma to sway others.

claims.title: One converts, Eight overpowers
claims.content: Enneagram Type One tries to convert people who resist it, while Enneagram Type Eight tries to power through them.

claims.title: One drives points despite conflict
claims.content: Enneagram Type One puts principle first and will drive its point home to convert others, even if this causes upsets or arguments.

claims.title: Eights mistaken for Ones
claims.content: Other people sometimes mistake Enneagram Type Eights for Ones because they see Eights as reformers.

claims.title: Eight justice for own people
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight seeks justice mainly for its own people, such as family, friends, coworkers, and ethnic group.

claims.title: Nine avoids conflict
claims.content: Average Enneagram Type Nines want to maintain peace and generally avoid arguing about convictions, especially with emotionally close people.

claims.title: Shared One and Nine traits
claims.content: Enneagram Type One and Type Nine can both be idealistic, philosophical, and somewhat withdrawn, and neither feels comfortable with its anger.

claims.title: Eight justice as reaction
claims.content: For Enneagram Type Eight, justice is a visceral reaction to witnessing injustice rather than an abstract principle.

claims.title: Celebrity examples for Ones and Nines
claims.content: The source gives Ted Koppel and Meryl Streep as examples of Type One, and Walter Cronkite and Andie MacDowell as examples of Type Nine.

claims.title: Three stress path toward Nine
claims.content: Under stress, Enneagram Threes keep driving themselves to excel until they burn out and become more detached and passive as they move toward Type Nine.

claims.title: Fives cope by isolating
claims.content: Enneagram Fives cope with rejection by detaching from the hurt and isolating themselves further.

claims.title: Stressed Fours show Two-like behaviors
claims.content: Some Fours who have been under stress for some time may recognize many Two-like behaviors in themselves.

claims.title: Charm blurs 2W3 and 3W2
claims.content: Personal charm and the desire to be liked and to please others can make the 2W3 and 3W2 types harder to distinguish.

claims.title: Two stress path toward Eight
claims.content: Under stress, Enneagram Twos keep doing nice things for others until they lose patience and blow up as they move toward Type Eight.

claims.title: Celebrity examples for Twos and Fives
claims.content: The source gives Barry Manilow and T. Berry Brazelton as examples of Type Two, and Philip Glass and Oliver Sacks as examples of Type Five.

claims.title: Twos move toward others
claims.content: Enneagram Twos tend to move toward others and engage them, sometimes excessively.

claims.title: Needy Fives may resemble Twos
claims.content: Some Enneagram Fives may be mistaken for Twos only in narrow circumstances, when they are highly dependent on the few people they bond with and become needy with significant others.

claims.title: Twos and Fives feel rejection
claims.content: Enneagram Twos and Fives both feel rejected easily.

claims.title: One stress path toward Four
claims.content: Under stress, Enneagram Type One first becomes more fervent in trying to convince others it is right, then collapses into moodiness and tight-lipped testiness as it moves toward Type Four.

claims.title: Twos irritated by intellectual approaches
claims.content: Enneagram Twos go by their feelings and can get flustered or irritated by overly intellectual approaches or complex ideas and procedures.

claims.title: Celebrity examples for Twos and Threes
claims.content: The source gives Stevie Wonder and Jerry Lewis as examples of Type Two, and Sting and Dick Clark as examples of Type Three.

claims.title: Celebrity examples for Twos and Fours
claims.content: The source gives Bill Cosby and Sally Struthers as examples of Type Two, and James Dean and Judy Garland as examples of Type Four.

claims.title: Twos cope by winning people over
claims.content: Enneagram Twos cope with rejection by winning people over.

claims.title: Threes fear intimacy
claims.content: Enneagram Threes enjoy attention and want relationships, but they fear intimacy and become more uneasy as relationships grow closer.

claims.title: Two and Five self-mistyping is rare
claims.content: Few people of either Enneagram Type Two or Type Five would be likely to mistype themselves as the other type.

claims.title: Twos are openly sentimental
claims.content: Enneagram Twos are openly sentimental and emote easily.

claims.title: Twos and Fives are near opposites
claims.content: Enneagram Twos are emotionally expressive and highly people-oriented, while Fives are emotionally detached.

claims.title: Twos attuned to others, not self
claims.content: Enneagram Twos are very aware of others' feelings but tend to be unaware of their own motivations and needs.

claims.title: Romanticism can lead to mistyping
claims.content: Twos who see themselves as romantic may mistype as Fours, because Fours are described as romantic.

claims.title: Twos win others through attention
claims.content: Enneagram Twos try to get others to like them by doing good things for them and focusing attention on the other person.

claims.title: Twos hesitate to pursue goals
claims.content: Enneagram Twos can be ambitious but feel uncomfortable pursuing their goals directly, believing that would be too selfish.

claims.title: Fours attuned to own emotions
claims.content: Enneagram Fours are highly attuned to their own emotional states but can fail to recognize their impact on others.

claims.title: Depression does not indicate a type
claims.content: All nine Enneagram types can be depressed, so feeling sad or alienated does not indicate any particular type.

claims.title: Rescuer roles of Twos and Fours
claims.content: Enneagram Twos look for people to rescue, while Fours look for someone to rescue them.

claims.title: Wings reduce Two and Three mix-ups
claims.content: A Two with a One-wing is unlikely to be mistyped as a Three, and a Three with a Four-wing is unlikely to be mistaken for a Two.

claims.title: Fours withdraw and wait
claims.content: Enneagram Fours tend to withdraw from others while hoping that others will seek them out.

claims.title: Threes are composed
claims.content: Enneagram Threes tend to be composed and have difficulty accessing their feelings.

claims.title: Threes are goal-driven
claims.content: Enneagram Threes are extremely goal-driven and feel they are not living up to their potential if they are not the best at what they do.

claims.title: Fives form bonds slowly
claims.content: Enneagram Fives do not form emotional bonds easily.

claims.title: Nine stress path toward Six
claims.content: Under stress, Enneagram Type Nine first becomes more emotionally disengaged and resistant, then more anxious and reactive as it moves toward Type Six.

claims.title: Female Fours may identify as Twos
claims.content: Female Fours reared in traditional or strongly religious environments may identify themselves as Twos, and this mistyping risk applies to women of all types.

claims.title: Twos seek closeness through pleasing
claims.content: Enneagram Twos are primarily motivated by the desire to please others as a way of creating closeness or intimacy.

claims.title: Seductiveness is not unique to Twos
claims.content: All types can be seductive in their own way, so the word seductive does not uniquely identify Enneagram Type Two.

claims.title: Threes win others through excellence
claims.content: Enneagram Threes get others to like them by developing the excellence of their own presentation, seldom lavishing attention on others.

claims.title: Two and Four mix-ups stem from narrow definitions
claims.content: Twos and Fours are seldom mistaken for each other, and when they are, it is usually because the types are defined too narrowly.

claims.title: Twos and Fours share feeling focus
claims.content: Enneagram Twos and Fours can be confused because both are Feeling types and both emphasize the ups and downs of personal relationships.

claims.title: Fives at home with intellectual complexity
claims.content: Enneagram Fives get flustered or irritated by sentimentality and gushiness, and they are in their element with intellectual concepts and complexity.

claims.title: Depression can lead Twos to mistype
claims.content: Some Twos may mistype themselves as Fours after a depression or the end of an important relationship, having learned that Fours are a depressive type.

claims.title: Twos want to be needed
claims.content: Average Twos want others to need them, while average Sevens do not want to be needed by anyone.

claims.title: Twos seek love and importance
claims.content: Twos want to be loved and to be important to others.

claims.title: Sixes seek approval and support
claims.content: Sixes want the approval and support of others.

claims.title: Sixes fear and increase dependence
claims.content: Average to unhealthy Sixes increasingly fear becoming dependent on others while actually becoming more dependent.

claims.title: Twos and Sixes often mistyped
claims.content: Twos and Sixes are a common mistype because they share several key traits.

claims.title: Seven emotions more labile
claims.content: The emotions of Sevens are more labile than the feelings of Twos.

claims.title: Unhealthy Twos become manipulative
claims.content: As they deteriorate, average to unhealthy Twos become increasingly covert and ultimately manipulative, concealing their true motives even from themselves.

claims.title: Twos do not consult authority
claims.content: Twos are not as indecisive or doubt-ridden as Sixes and do not consult an authority figure for answers.

claims.title: Average Twos effusive and warm
claims.content: Average Twos are friendly and effusive, sometimes gushy and dramatic, and they take pains to express warm, personal appreciation of others.

claims.title: Twos believe love comes from dependence
claims.content: Average to unhealthy Twos believe they will only get love by having others depend on them.

claims.title: Labile: changing quickly
claims.content: Labile means changing quickly, as used to describe emotions.

claims.title: Sevens enjoy company for activities
claims.content: Sevens do not like to eat, drink, go to the theater, or go on vacation alone, because their activities are more enjoyable when others are present.

claims.title: Twos' feelings tied to self
claims.content: Twos' feelings are intimately connected with their sense of self, their behavior, and their interactions with others.

claims.title: Sevens' flamboyant, varied emotions
claims.content: Average Sevens dramatize their emotions flamboyantly, and these emotions are usually shorter lived and wide-ranging, from elation and giddiness to rage.

claims.title: Six as introverted feeling
claims.content: The Six is the introverted feeling type in Jungian typology.

claims.title: Twos more low-keyed
claims.content: Twos are more low-keyed than Sevens; unless they are very unhealthy, Twos do not express anger at others as openly, and they never display the range of emotions Sevens show.

claims.title: Average Twos offer rather than seek
claims.content: Average Twos ingratiate themselves from an implied position of superiority, offering love, approval, and advice rather than seeking them, at least at first.

claims.title: Sixes select, Twos sweep
claims.content: Sixes warily invite selected others into their lives, while Twos throw out the net of their feelings and see whom they can sweep into the fold.

claims.title: Sixes send mixed signals
claims.content: Sixes are often ambivalent about their feelings and frequently send ambiguous, mixed signals to other people.

claims.title: Sevens as free-floating adventurers
claims.content: Sevens do not get as involved in other people's lives and see themselves as members of a free-floating band of fellow adventurers, not the center of a family or community.

claims.title: Sevens' generosity serves own enjoyment
claims.content: Sevens may pay for others' tickets or meals, but their motives often have more to do with their own enjoyment than with helping needier friends.

claims.title: Sixes want independence within partnerships
claims.content: Sixes want partnerships that support their bid for independence, but they become anxious if a relationship becomes too merged or mushy.

claims.title: Two as extroverted feeling
claims.content: The Two is the extroverted feeling type in Jungian typology.

claims.title: Twos want significance, may meddle
claims.content: Twos want to be significant to others and on intimate terms with them, although they sometimes meddle too much and are too solicitous to make sure they are needed.

claims.title: Unhealthy Sixes become paranoid
claims.content: As they deteriorate, average to unhealthy Sixes become wildly reactive, consciously confused about their feelings, and ultimately paranoid.

claims.title: Twos want intimacy and merging
claims.content: Twos want to be close to others, and the more intimacy and merging they have with loved ones, the better.

claims.title: Sixes ingratiate through playful teasing
claims.content: Sixes ingratiate themselves by being playful and silly and by bantering and teasing people they want to draw a protective emotional response from.

claims.title: Twos and Sevens often mistaken
claims.content: Twos and Sevens are often mistaken because both can be emotional and histrionic.

claims.title: Average Twos become advisers
claims.content: As they grow in self-importance, average Twos usually make themselves authority figures, dispensing advice on all life issues to people within their spheres of influence.

claims.title: Twos openly demonstrative
claims.content: Twos wear their hearts on their sleeves and are openly warm and demonstrative about how they feel toward others.

claims.title: Sixes seek authority reassurance
claims.content: Sixes are consciously assailed by anxiety, indecision, and doubts, and they look to trusted others, especially authority figures, for reassurance and confidence.

claims.title: Contrast of unhealthy Two and Six
claims.content: At the end of the Continuum, unhealthy Twos show psychosomatic suffering and romantic obsession, while unhealthy Sixes show paranoia and volatile lashing out.

claims.title: Eights direct, Twos indirect anger
claims.content: Eights express anger and disappointment openly and directly, while Twos have great difficulty communicating anger openly and use indirect approaches.

claims.title: Twos possessive of friends
claims.content: Average Twos are possessive of friends because they have invested time and emotional energy and do not want them to drift away.

claims.title: Sevens misidentifying as Twos
claims.content: More Sevens misidentify themselves as Twos than the reverse.

claims.title: Twos and Eights share rejection feelings
claims.content: Both Twos and Eights struggle with underlying feelings of rejection, but they cope with them differently.

claims.title: Nines and Twos love differently
claims.content: Twos and Nines both focus on others' needs and service, but Nines are self-effacing and content to support others without seeking much attention in return.

claims.title: Nines mistaken for Twos
claims.content: Average Nines often mistakenly think they are Twos, while average Twos rarely misidentify themselves as Nines.

claims.title: Nines need fewer responses
claims.content: Average Nines are patient about wanting their love returned and can be satisfied with fewer responses than Twos.

claims.title: Two's Direction of Disintegration is Eight
claims.content: Eight is the Direction of Disintegration for Type Two, and stressed Twos increasingly resemble Eights.

claims.title: Twos and Eights confusion
claims.content: Twos and Eights can be confused because both are forceful and dominating, though Twos often express this covertly.

claims.title: Twos perceive others' hurts
claims.content: Average Twos have an acute sense of other people's hurts, needs, and frailties.

claims.title: Twos versus Sevens: thinking or feeling
claims.content: Twos and Sevens are often confused, but Sevens are primarily thinking types while Twos are feeling types.

claims.title: Twos use guilt when frustrated
claims.content: When frustrated, Twos try to make others feel guilty by dramatizing their suffering and try to control others to prevent them from leaving.

claims.title: Nines idealize partners
claims.content: Average Nines tend to idealize others and fall in love with an idealized version of the person rather than the person as they are.

claims.title: Sevens end relationships quickly
claims.content: Average Sevens are less attached to people and end relationships fairly quickly once they decide the relationship is not working.

claims.title: Twos struggle to let go
claims.content: Twos have more difficulty letting go of relationships than Sevens do.

claims.title: Average Twos: need to be needed
claims.content: Average Twos need to be needed and want people to come to them for approval, guidance, and advice.

claims.title: Fours: process feelings first
claims.content: Fours want to stop what they are doing and process difficult feelings before returning to their tasks.

claims.title: Fives: process-oriented thinking
claims.content: Fives are process-oriented and can pursue abstract ideas for knowledge itself, without caring about final goals.

claims.title: Average Twos: self-awareness
claims.content: Average Twos have a sharp sense of their own identities and are highly aware of their feelings and virtues.

claims.title: Average Threes: feelings deprioritized
claims.content: Average Threes tend to put their feelings aside to focus on tasks, efficiency, and performance.

claims.title: Threes mistyping as Fives
claims.content: Some average Threes mistype as Fives because they want to see themselves as thinkers.

claims.title: Healthy Twos: personal help
claims.content: Healthy Twos help others with a direct, personal focus that responds to each person's own needs.

claims.title: Fives are loners, indifferent to image
claims.content: Fives are usually loners who put little effort into their appearance and care little about others' opinions.

claims.title: Sevens sense of self from stimulation
claims.content: Sevens maintain their sense of self by acquiring things and experiences that stimulate them, whether or not others know about them.

claims.title: Threes and Sixes share work focus
claims.content: Threes and Sixes are not often mistyped, but both are very focused on work and performance.

claims.title: Fives persist with long projects
claims.content: Average Fives may stay with a project for years until they exhaust their subject, themselves, or both.

claims.title: Seven and Three confusion source
claims.content: Traditional Enneagram teaching confuses Sevens and Threes partly because unhealthy Sevens in a manic phase have grandiose delusions similar to narcissistic Threes' grandiose self-esteem.

claims.title: Threes example public figures
claims.content: Michael Tilson Thomas and Carl Sagan are cited as examples of Threes.

claims.title: Threes use status for self-worth
claims.content: For Threes, status symbols reinforce their feeling of self-worth and sense of self.

claims.title: Fives example public figures
claims.content: Glenn Gould and Stanley Kubrick are cited as examples of Fives.

claims.title: Threes present themselves well
claims.content: Threes are highly sociable and well groomed, and they know how to present themselves favorably.

claims.title: Threes and Sixes example figures
claims.content: Tom Cruise and Whitney Houston are cited as examples of Threes, and Tom Hanks and Bonnie Raitt as examples of Sixes.

claims.title: Threes share achievements, Fives conceal
claims.content: Average Threes tend to talk about their achievements, while average Fives tend to be secretive about their work and discoveries.

claims.title: Threes reserved, Sixes intense
claims.content: Threes project cool emotional reserve, while Sixes project more volatile and intense feelings.

claims.title: Fives pursue knowledge for itself
claims.content: Average Fives pursue knowledge for its own sake, not for practical results, fame or fortune.

claims.title: Cruise meaning differs for Sevens and Threes
claims.content: A first-class cruise gives Sevens pleasure regardless of who knows, while for Threes it symbolizes having arrived at success.

claims.title: Threes seek spotlight, Sixes avoid it
claims.content: Threes see themselves as soloists who want to excel and need recognition, while Sixes feel awkward taking the spotlight unless they move to Three under stress.

claims.title: Threes pursue work for recognition
claims.content: Average Threes often undertake intellectual work to reach long-range goals and gain recognition, not for love of knowledge.

claims.title: Eight self-assertion and quick compliance
claims.content: Average Eights are self-assertive and want others to give in to them immediately so they do not have to waste time fighting.

claims.title: Power versus worth motives
claims.content: Eights seek personal power as their dominant drive, while Threes seek enough success and prestige to feel valuable and worthy.

claims.title: Emotional tone of Threes and Sevens
claims.content: Average Threes appear cool, in control, and free of emotional problems, while average Sevens have more rough edges and seem less self-contained.

claims.title: Shared ambition of Threes and Eights
claims.content: Threes and Eights are both ambitious and competitive, and both want to rise above others.

claims.title: Failure as humiliation or learning
claims.content: Threes fear failure as personal humiliation and rejection as worthless, while Eights see failure as an opportunity to learn and return stronger.

claims.title: Shared adaptability of Threes and Nines
claims.content: Threes and Nines are both highly adaptable and can both seek acceptance from others, and both can have trouble recognizing who they are or what they want.

claims.title: Eight competition areas
claims.content: Eights compete for material, political, or sexual dominance, and less over purely social or status issues.

claims.title: Seven versus Three narcissism
claims.content: Average Sevens are not narcissistic in the classic sense and are not particularly vulnerable to narcissistic hurt, while Threes are classic narcissists.

claims.title: Seven and Three grandiosity differ
claims.content: Average Sevens are grandiose about their plans, while average Threes are grandiose about their ability to achieve things.

claims.title: Seven self-expression without censorship
claims.content: Average Sevens do not censor themselves and can be funny, outspoken, vulgar, ill mannered, and outrageous in public.

claims.title: Three self-starting motivation
claims.content: Threes are highly motivated self-starters who launch into projects with a sense that they can and will succeed.

claims.title: Pressure handling of Threes and Eights
claims.content: Average Threes cannot sustain pressure or open confrontation for long and turn to diplomacy or covert retaliation, while average Eights take the heat.

claims.title: Grandiosity motives for Sevens and Threes
claims.content: When grandiose, Sevens try to escape pain and anxiety, while grandiose Threes overcompensate for their fear of failure.

claims.title: Three resemblance to Nine in disintegration
claims.content: Threes can resemble Nines when they move to Nine in their Direction of Disintegration, becoming more disengaged and unmotivated by their usual goals.

claims.title: Unhealthy Three self-grandiosity
claims.content: Unhealthy Threes are grandiose about their self-worth and are narcissistic, exhibitionistic, and prone to exaggerating their accomplishments.

claims.title: Dependence on others' opinions
claims.content: Threes depend on others' opinions and want to be in social demand, while Eights do not care about popularity as long as they get their way.

claims.title: Sixes: relating to people
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six individuals relate well to people and unconsciously engage others' emotions so that others like them and form secure relationships with them.

claims.title: Fours: emotional volatility
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four individuals are self-absorbed and emotionally volatile, and they need others to respond to them emotionally.

claims.title: Sixes: depression from fear of anger
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six individuals become depressed when they fear that they have made their allies or authority figures angry with them.

claims.title: Fours and Sixes: depression roots
claims.content: Depression in Enneagram Type Six individuals is based on repressed anxiety, while depression in Enneagram Type Four individuals is based on repressed hatred toward the self and others.

claims.title: Fives: inner emptiness
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five individuals tend to focus on inner emptiness and feelings of meaninglessness.

claims.title: Fives: vision-based art
claims.content: The artistic work of Enneagram Type Five individuals is less autobiographical and more often portrays their vision of reality.

claims.title: Fives mistyped as Fours
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five individuals are more likely to be mistyped as Enneagram Type Four than the reverse, mainly because of simplistic type definitions.

claims.title: Fours: focus on inner states
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four individuals do not relate primarily to other people but to their own inner emotional states.

claims.title: Threes and Nines: sources of excitement
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three individuals get excited about their projects, while Enneagram Type Nine individuals get excited about their free time and comforts.

claims.title: Nines: goals and slowing down
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine individuals are determined to meet their goals and have trouble slowing down and relaxing.

claims.title: Fours: depression from self-disappointment
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four individuals become depressed when they are disappointed with themselves for losing an opportunity to actualize themselves.

claims.title: Fours: focus on past pain
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four individuals tend to focus on disappointments in love and on their childhoods and the pain attached to them.

claims.title: Threes: seeking attention
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three individuals try to garner attention from people they believe are important to them.

claims.title: Ambivert: definition
claims.content: An ambivert is a person who has qualities of both introversion and extroversion.

claims.title: Fours and Sixes: orientation
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four individuals are true introverts, while Enneagram Type Six individuals blend introversion and extroversion.

claims.title: Nines: support for goals
claims.content: Many highly accomplished Enneagram Type Nine individuals have friends or spouses who keep them motivated and on track with their goals.

claims.title: Fours and Fives: shared traits
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four and Type Five individuals can both be withdrawn, individualistic, eccentric by mainstream standards, and highly creative.

claims.title: Nines: reluctance to seek attention
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine individuals are reluctant to ask for attention and discount themselves easily.

claims.title: Fours: autobiographical art
claims.content: The artistic work of Enneagram Type Four individuals tends to be autobiographical, based on their families, relationships, and subjective experience.

claims.title: Artistic talent across types
claims.content: Artistic talent is not limited to Enneagram Type Four individuals, so Enneagram Type Six individuals can also be artists.

claims.title: Nines: self-care and relaxing
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine individuals generally have trouble doing good things for themselves but relax more easily than Enneagram Type Three individuals.

claims.title: Fives and Fours: drives compared
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five individuals are driven to penetrate the surface of things to understand them, while Enneagram Type Four individuals seek to get in touch with feelings and express them cathartically.

claims.title: Sensuality motives differ by type
claims.content: Sevens use sensuality to stay happy and avoid anxiety and negative feelings, while Fours use it to heighten emotional fantasies and deaden the pain of self-consciousness.

claims.title: Fours and Sevens differ greatly
claims.content: Sevens and Fours are vastly different, and their only notable similarity is excessiveness at Level 6 of both types.

claims.title: Fours comfortable with sadness
claims.content: Fours feel comfortable with sadness and pain because these feelings are an important part of their identities.

claims.title: Sevens lose interest after acquiring
claims.content: Sevens are excited mainly by the stimulation of desiring something new, and usually lose interest once they have acquired it.

claims.title: Sevens at Level 6
claims.content: At Level 6, Sevens become jaded, hardened, insensitive, demanding, selfish, and uncaring about others.

claims.title: Fours value personal truth
claims.content: For Fours, personal truth matters more than tradition, and tradition serves only as a backdrop for their personal dramas.

claims.title: Sevens versus Fours temperament
claims.content: Average Sevens tend to be upbeat experience-seekers, while average Fours tend to be languishing aesthetes.

claims.title: Fours value beauty over possessions
claims.content: Fours cherish beautiful objects for their beauty and the feelings it awakens, and can be satisfied by small items such as a stone or a twig.

claims.title: Self-Indulgent Aesthete label
claims.content: The Self-Indulgent Aesthete is the label for Fours at the same level, whose excess is emotional and centered on their inner world of feelings and fantasies.

claims.title: Themes in Sixes' art
claims.content: The art of Sixes typically addresses belonging, security, family, politics, country, and common values.

claims.title: Sevens mistaken for Fours
claims.content: Sevens may be mistaken for Fours because they suffer depression, but they quickly seek positive activities and can become manic to avoid painful feelings.

claims.title: Fours explore personal feelings
claims.content: Creative Fours are individualists who explore their own feelings and subjective personal states, and their art is much less tied to tradition or rebellion against it.

claims.title: Sixes tend toward performing arts
claims.content: Average Sixes tend to be performing artists, more often actors or musicians than poets and playwrights.

claims.title: Sixes relate to tradition
claims.content: Creative Sixes tend either to work within established traditions or to rebel against them, and tradition matters to their art either way.

claims.title: Fours indulge in emotion
claims.content: Average Fours wallow in their feelings and fantasies, pursuing intense emotional charges even when they are unrealistic or emotionally debilitating.

claims.title: Excessive Materialist label
claims.content: The Excessive Materialist is the label for Sevens, whose excess is in the external, material world of possessions and experiences.

claims.title: Sevens acquire for security
claims.content: Average Sevens become increasingly unappreciative of the beauty of objects they acquire, and acquire possessions mainly for a sense of security.

claims.title: Fours are highly resilient
claims.content: Fours are highly resilient and can endure emotional difficulties and losses that would cause most other types to collapse.

claims.title: Fours and tragic themes
claims.content: Fours often deal in tragic themes, finding redemption in understanding loss and sorrow.

claims.title: Nines and commonplace comfort
claims.content: Nines deal in the commonplace, finding comfort in ordinary lives, simple situations, or reassuring fantasy.

claims.title: Nines dissociate, Fours brood
claims.content: Average to unhealthy Nines tune out unpleasantness by dissociating, while Fours brood over their hurts to come to terms with them.

claims.title: Sixes mistyped as Fives
claims.content: Sixes are more often mistyped as Fives than Fives are mistyped as Sixes.

claims.title: Nines withdraw to avoid anxiety
claims.content: Nines withdraw by removing their attention from people or situations that threaten them, disengaging emotionally to avoid anxiety or upset.

claims.title: Eights cope by toughening up
claims.content: Eights cope with childhood hurts by toughening up and getting over them to keep their independence and personal authority.

claims.title: Eights as inverted Fours
claims.content: Eights are like Fours turned inside out.

claims.title: Fours tougher than they realize
claims.content: Fours show their vulnerability but can be tougher and more controlling than they generally realize.

claims.title: Fives trust only own minds
claims.content: Fives trust only their own minds to reach conclusions and believe others are likely less well informed.

claims.title: Nines mistaken for Fours
claims.content: Some average Nines think they are Fours because they have artistic talents or creative inclinations.

claims.title: Sixes think linearly
claims.content: Sixes think in linear, analytical ways, focusing on troubleshooting, prediction, and repeatable methods.

claims.title: Eights mistaken for Fours
claims.content: Eights often mistake themselves for Fours because both feel passionate and intense.

claims.title: Fives think nonlinearly
claims.content: Fives think nonlinearly, seeking where established theories break down and developing ideas that challenge established methods.

claims.title: Fives bolder, less practical
claims.content: Fives are bolder than Sixes in their positions and creativity but are less practical.

claims.title: Fours and Nines both withdraw
claims.content: Fours and Nines are both withdrawn types, which is the main reason they may be confused.

claims.title: Nine art versus Four art
claims.content: The art of Nines often expresses idealized, mythological, and archetypal worlds, while the art of Fours is more personal and self-revealing.

claims.title: Fours hold onto childhood wounds
claims.content: Fours find it difficult to let go of their childhood wounds and do not want to get over them.

claims.title: Nines detached, Fours withdrawn
claims.content: Nines are detached from both the outside world and their emotions, while Fours withdraw from whatever has caused them pain.

claims.title: Fours withdraw to process emotions
claims.content: Fours withdraw from others to give themselves time to deal with their emotions.

claims.title: Nines have diffuse sense of self
claims.content: Average Nines have little sense of who they are apart from the people and types they identify with.

claims.title: Sevens optimistic, Fives drawn to dark
claims.content: Sevens are optimists who avoid dark, painful, or heavy topics, while Fives are drawn to the dark, macabre, and nihilistic side of life.

claims.title: Average Fives suspicious of people
claims.content: Average Fives are suspicious of people and are not trusting, sometimes too cynical and resistant.

claims.title: Fives under stress resemble Sevens
claims.content: Under increased stress, Fives can become distracted and scattered like average Sevens, and they return to focused, withdrawn ways once the stress is relieved.

claims.title: Fives and Nines share schizoid defense
claims.content: Fives and Nines both use a schizoid defense of the self, detaching from their feelings, though their similarities are only superficial.

claims.title: Sixes seek trust in others
claims.content: Sixes look for something to trust because they do not trust their own minds to reach meaningful conclusions.

claims.title: Eco and Clancy as type examples
claims.content: Umberto Eco, a Five, and Tom Clancy, a Six, illustrate the difference between Fives and Sixes.

claims.title: Fives and Eights feel outsider
claims.content: Fives and Eights both see themselves as outsiders and easily feel rejected.

claims.title: Gifts of Fives and Sevens
claims.content: The gift of the Five is intense focus and concentration, while the gift of the Seven is breadth of vision and synthesis.

claims.title: Fives head-centered, ambivalent about body
claims.content: Fives tend to stay in their heads, often have an ambivalent relationship with their bodies, and find staying grounded and practical a problem.

claims.title: Fives and Sevens share curiosity
claims.content: Fives and Sevens are both thinking types that are highly curious, exploratory, and willing to try new ways of doing things.

claims.title: Nines gentle, Fives intense
claims.content: Nines are gentle, easygoing, patient, and accommodating, while Fives are intense, strong-minded, high-strung, and argumentative.

claims.title: Nines mistaking themselves for Fives
claims.content: Average Nines often mistakenly think they are Fives, particularly average male Nines who are well educated and intelligent.

claims.title: Eights instinctual and practical
claims.content: Eights are highly instinctual and intimately related to their bodies, which makes them people of practical action, pragmatism, and sensuality.

claims.title: Fives withdrawn, Sevens gregarious
claims.content: Fives tend to be more socially isolated and withdrawn than Sevens, who are highly gregarious and like to stay active.

claims.title: Nines avoid typing due to anxiety
claims.content: Average Nines avoid identifying their type because doing so arouses anxiety, and they prefer maintaining emotional comfort over deeper insight.

claims.title: Sixes respond to anxiety
claims.content: Enneagram Sixes are driven by anxiety, often fretting, becoming more anxious, or reacting counter-phobically against their fears.

claims.title: Famous examples of Fives and Nines
claims.content: Charles Darwin and Albert Einstein are given as examples of Enneagram Fives, and Walt Disney and Jim Henson as examples of Nines.

claims.title: Sixes and Sevens mistyping
claims.content: Enneagram Sixes and Sevens can be mistyped when people confuse a main type with its wing.

claims.title: Fives block out other perceptions
claims.content: Enneagram Fives concentrate so intensely in their thinking that they block out other perceptions, eventually to their detriment.

claims.title: Fives distort reality at extremes
claims.content: At an extreme, Enneagram Fives may see reality as a projection of their preoccupations and fears, making it seem more negative and threatening than it is.

claims.title: Fives' intellectual defense
claims.content: Enneagram Fives fear being overwhelmed by the world, and their intellectual efforts are an unconscious defense to master it.

claims.title: Nines and Fives communicate differently
claims.content: Enneagram Nines may be gifted storytellers who communicate simply and effectively, while Fives usually communicate with only a few people or keep ideas to themselves.

claims.title: Common Six misidentifications listed
claims.content: Enneagram Sixes are commonly misidentified as Ones, Twos, Threes, Fours, or Fives.

claims.title: Fives pursue grand unifying theories
claims.content: Average Enneagram Fives pursue a grand unifying theory and become involved in increasing complications and abstractions.

claims.title: Nines' attention drifts easily
claims.content: Enneagram Nines tend to lose concentration and interest quickly, letting attention drift when bored or anxious.

claims.title: Fives' concentrated thinking style
claims.content: Enneagram Fives think in a highly concentrated, penetrating way, focused on specifics.

claims.title: Nines simplify reality comfortingly
claims.content: Enneagram Nines tend to simplify reality and reinterpret it to make it more comforting and less threatening.

claims.title: Fives predict consequences
claims.content: Enneagram Fives are extremely interested in predicting the consequences of every action, while Nines usually do not consider consequences.

claims.title: Sixes' anxiety-driven pessimism
claims.content: Anxiety tends to make Enneagram Sixes more pessimistic and negative about themselves and their prospects, with self-doubt and suspicion of others' motives.

claims.title: Nines' impressionistic thinking style
claims.content: Enneagram Nines think in an impressionistic way, focused on generalities, synthesis, imaginative ruminations, and fanciful situations.

claims.title: Intelligence does not indicate Five
claims.content: Intelligence alone does not make an Enneagram Nine a Five.

claims.title: Nines feel at ease
claims.content: Enneagram Nines feel at ease in the world, and their thinking style reflects an unconscious desire to merge with the world.

claims.title: Thinking alone is insufficient
claims.content: Thinking alone, without further distinction, is not a sufficient basis for a personality diagnosis.

claims.title: Level 6: Sixes and Eights compared
claims.content: At Level 6, unhealthy Sixes and Eights show similar aggressive traits, but Eights arrive there by escalating pressure on others.

claims.title: Nines under stress: mistyping risk
claims.content: Under stress, Nines may briefly act like average Sixes, which can lead some Nines to mistype themselves as Sixes, but such anxiety generally does not last long.

claims.title: Sixes and Sevens: structure preference
claims.content: Sixes seek out structure and guidelines, while Sevens resist both structure and guidelines.

claims.title: Unhealthy Sixes and Eights: danger
claims.content: Unhealthy Eights are more dangerous than unhealthy Sixes because they are more ruthless, while unhealthy Sixes tend to become self-defeating.

claims.title: Sevens: commonly confused types
claims.content: Sevens are often misidentified as Ones, Twos, Threes, Fours, Fives, or Sixes, and the source cross-references each of these pairs.

claims.title: Sixes and Eights: aggression level
claims.content: Sixes and Eights are both aggressive, but only Eights are entirely aggressive personalities.

claims.title: Sixes and Nines: trust and venting
claims.content: Sixes need to vent with others and test people before trusting them, while Nines tend to trust others almost to a fault.

claims.title: Sixes and Eights: response to pressure
claims.content: Sixes become aggressive to avoid being pushed around, and their defenses crumble under enough pressure, while pressure makes Eights more defiant.

claims.title: Sixes and Nines: affect difference
claims.content: Sixes and Nines are most easily distinguished by affect: Nines stay easygoing and unflappable, while Sixes become agitated and rattled by mishaps.

claims.title: Sevens and Sixes: handling dark feelings
claims.content: Sevens tend to deny the dark corners of their souls, while Sixes tend to get stuck in them.

claims.title: Eights decide by gut instinct
claims.content: Eights are instinctive types who make decisions from their gut instincts.

claims.title: Energy levels of Sevens and Nines
claims.content: Average Sevens are hyperactive extroverts, while average Nines are more easygoing and live at a much lower energy level.

claims.title: Celebrity examples of Sevens and Eights
claims.content: Mike Myers and Goldie Hawn are cited as examples of Sevens, and Danny DeVito and Roseanne Barr as examples of Eights.

claims.title: Sevens and Eights both aggressive
claims.content: Sevens and Eights are both aggressive types who are powerful and able to go after what they want.

claims.title: Nines seek placid contentment
claims.content: Nines seek placid contentment, being neither too excited nor in discomfort, rather than the euphoria and elation that Sevens seek.

claims.title: Sevens are thinking types
claims.content: Sevens are thinking types who can have brilliant, quick minds.

claims.title: Eights value power for independence
claims.content: Eights are interested in power as a way to maintain their independence and assert their dominance in the environment.

claims.title: Nines stay busy to avoid anxiety
claims.content: Nines are highly intolerant of anxiety and stay busy with undemanding, nonthreatening errands and hobbies to avoid it.

claims.title: Nines introvert on union sensation
claims.content: Nines orient themselves to the world by introverting on the sensation of union with another person, introjecting that person and idealizing the introjection.

claims.title: Sevens seek variety of experiences
claims.content: Sevens are primarily interested in variety and want to sample as many different experiences as possible.

claims.title: Emotional involvement in activities
claims.content: Average Nines do not want to be emotionally involved in their activities, since these can threaten their identifications, whereas Sevens want an increasingly high emotional charge from their activities.

claims.title: Stimulation: Sevens versus Nines
claims.content: Sevens want to be stimulated and love excitement, while Nines want to avoid anything that would overly stimulate or upset them.

claims.title: Self-views of Sevens and Eights
claims.content: Sevens see themselves as idealistic optimists, while Eights see themselves as hard-nosed realists.

claims.title: Eights seek intense experiences
claims.content: Eights are primarily interested in intensity and care more about having intense experiences they enjoy than about variety.

claims.title: Sevens avoid power for freedom
claims.content: Sevens are not particularly interested in having power because maintaining it may infringe on their freedom.

claims.title: Sevens struggle to stay focused
claims.content: Sevens can get ahead of themselves with their plans, schemes, and interests, and can have trouble staying grounded and focused on their projects.

claims.title: Nines define self through others
claims.content: Nines maintain their sense of self by living through an identification with another person.

claims.title: Sevens and Nines in Jungian model
claims.content: Sevens correspond to the extroverted sensation type in the Jungian model, and Nines correspond to the introverted sensation type.

claims.title: Shared repression of Sevens and Nines
claims.content: Sevens and Nines both repress the darker parts of their inner worlds: Nines to maintain idealized identifications with others, and Sevens to suppress overwhelming pain and anxiety.

claims.title: Nines cross-referenced with confused types
claims.content: The source cross-references Nines with the types they are often confused with: Twos, Threes, Fours, Fives, Sixes, Sevens, and Eights.

claims.title: Nine deterioration: passivity and depression
claims.content: As Nines deteriorate down the Levels, they become more passive, disengaged, and depressive.

claims.title: Feeling Center linked to emotion
claims.content: The Feeling Center is the intelligence of the heart and is associated with emotion and feelings.

claims.title: Eights are openly assertive
claims.content: Eights are openly assertive and do not mind debating to make their point.

claims.title: Centers operate simultaneously
claims.content: The three Centers operate simultaneously, and a response from any one Center causes the other two to actuate as well.

claims.title: Ego responds to stress with tension
claims.content: The ego responds to stress and threats by tensing and constricting the body and withdrawing attention from direct engagement with reality.

claims.title: Three Centers of human intelligence
claims.content: Human intelligence has three main Centers: the Instinctive Center, the Feeling Center, and the Thinking Center.

claims.title: Fear reinforces rigid boundaries
claims.content: Fear causes the ego to erect more rigid boundaries, further disengage from reality, and tense the body even more.

claims.title: Instinctive Center located in belly
claims.content: The Instinctive Center is the intelligence of the body or instincts and is traditionally located in the belly.

claims.title: Nines avoid contention
claims.content: Nines dislike contention of any kind and, if possible, would rather agree with others to keep the peace.

claims.title: Gurdjieff's names for the Centers
claims.content: Gurdjieff called the three Centers the Moving-Instinctive Center, the Emotional Center, and the Intellectual Center, corresponding to the Instinctive, Feeling, and Thinking Centers.

claims.title: Eight with Nine-wing mistyped as Nine
claims.content: An Eight with a Nine-wing can sometimes be mistaken for a Nine with an Eight-wing, although this mistype is not common.

claims.title: Eights seek and enjoy conflict
claims.content: Eights often seek conflicts and debates, and they find them energizing.

claims.title: Ego as self-reinforcing cat's cradle
claims.content: The ego structure is a self-reinforcing pattern of related reactions held in place by mutual tension, like a cat's cradle.

claims.title: Eight deterioration: anger and domination
claims.content: As Eights deteriorate down the Levels, they become more angry, aggressive, and domineering.

claims.title: Thinking Center covers cognition
claims.content: The Thinking Center is the intelligence of the head and encompasses the cognitive functions.

claims.title: Formatory apparatus definition
claims.content: Gurdjieff called the scrambling of the three lower Centers the formatory apparatus, which he said is the basis of personality.

claims.title: Scrambled lower Centers block higher signals
claims.content: Gurdjieff taught that the three lower Centers (instinctive, feeling, and thinking) become scrambled, which blocks signals from the higher Centers.

claims.title: House in disorder metaphor
claims.content: Gurdjieff described the human being as a house in disorder, like a mansion full of servants but without a master.

claims.title: Personality blocks Essential awareness
claims.content: The personality distorts the relationship between the Centers and prevents Essential awareness from restoring their proper function.

claims.title: Triads represent Essential qualities
claims.content: The three Triads represent three qualities of Essential Being that the personality tries to imitate.

claims.title: Higher Centers already operational
claims.content: Gurdjieff taught that the higher emotional and higher intellectual Centers are already operational and do not need to be developed.

claims.title: Personality as temporary patchwork
claims.content: From the perspective of Inner Work, the personality is a temporary patchwork that holds the Centers together until they can align more consciously.

claims.title: Scrambling passed through education
claims.content: Gurdjieff said the Centers are not naturally scrambled and become scrambled through education by people whose own Centers were scrambled.

claims.title: Essential qualities form a unity
claims.content: Groundedness in physicality, the opening of the heart, the quieting of the mind, and groundedness in Being form a unity, and none can function without the other two.

claims.title: Gurdjieff: ordinary consciousness outside Centers
claims.content: Gurdjieff taught that in ordinary ego consciousness, a person is not really in any of the three Centers: not really feeling, thinking, or present in the body.

claims.title: Shock points at Levels 3-4 and 6-7
claims.content: Shock points occur between the healthy and average ranges (Levels 3 and 4) and between the average and unhealthy ranges (Levels 6 and 7).

claims.title: Nine permutations behind Enneagram types
claims.content: Because there are three Centers, there are nine possible ways they can be scrambled, and the nine Enneagram personality types are based on these nine permutations.

claims.title: Third Center is undeveloped
claims.content: The third Center is undeveloped, largely unexplored territory that is not part of a person's ordinary self-image.

claims.title: M: Moving-Instinctive Center shorthand
claims.content: M is the shorthand for the function of Instinct, the Moving-Instinctive Center.

claims.title: Each shock point unbalances another Center
claims.content: At each shock point, as a person moves down the Levels, the personality knocks another Center out of balance.

claims.title: Centers affected by level range
claims.content: In the healthy range one Center is drawn on, in the average range two Centers are scrambled, and in the unhealthy range all three Centers are distorted.

claims.title: F: feeling function shorthand
claims.content: F is the shorthand for the function of feeling, the Feeling Center.

claims.title: Crossing shock points needs extremes
claims.content: Crossing a shock point in a lasting way usually requires extreme conditions or special intentions.

claims.title: Nines learn safe self-assertion
claims.content: Nines need to learn that they can assert themselves without losing their connection with others.

claims.title: Sixes learn safe inner guidance
claims.content: Sixes need to learn that they can follow their own inner guidance without losing support from others.

claims.title: Threes learn safe feeling
claims.content: Threes need to learn that they can feel their feelings without being rejected by others.

claims.title: Outside agent as temporary Center
claims.content: Unhealthy-range people may need an outside agent, such as a therapist or spiritual teacher, to serve temporarily as a stable Center to identify with.

claims.title: Primary types' therapy is harder at first
claims.content: Therapeutic work for primary types may be more difficult at first because they must directly confront problems in the fundamentally imbalanced Center.

claims.title: Primary and secondary types grow differently
claims.content: The primary types (Three, Six, and Nine) need a different approach to growth than the secondary types (One, Two, Four, Five, Seven, and Eight).

claims.title: Identification disconnects from conscious qualities
claims.content: Identification with the structures of the personality disconnects a person from many qualities that distinguish a conscious human being.

claims.title: Primary types work on boxed Center
claims.content: Primary types should work directly on the problematic Center that is boxed off from their other functions.

claims.title: Primary types' boxed Center explained
claims.content: In primary types, the problematic Center is segregated and out of communication with the other functions, not necessarily suppressed or broken.

claims.title: Diagram symbols for Center imbalance
claims.content: In the diagram, an underline marks the Center a type primarily identifies with, a box marks a Center segregated from the others, and a curved line marks linkage or scrambling between two Centers.

claims.title: T F M symbols show average-range imbalance
claims.content: The T F M letter sets with underlines, connecting lines, or boxes show each Enneagram type's imbalance of the three Centers in the average range.

claims.title: Personality sustained by Centers' energy
claims.content: The personality is an artificial construct that uses the energy of the Centers to sustain itself, and it both expresses and compensates for the Centers' imbalance.

claims.title: T: thinking function shorthand
claims.content: T is the shorthand for the function of thinking, the Thinking Center.

claims.title: Formatory apparatus defined
claims.content: Formatory apparatus is a mode of consciousness almost completely unrelated to what a person is actually experiencing in the present.

claims.title: Third Center problem only when unhealthy
claims.content: The third Center becomes a problem only in the unhealthy range, and it is not part of the picture in the average to healthy range.

claims.title: Average-range people start with third Center
claims.content: For people in the average range of their type, it is very helpful to work first on the third Center, the Center outside their typical identifications.

claims.title: Type Two expresses feelings through action
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two tends to express feelings through action, such as doing things for people, rather than feeling them directly.

claims.title: Imbalance of Centers as key
claims.content: Imbalance of Centers is described as the key to understanding personality structures and therapeutic strategies for unlocking them.

claims.title: Feeling Center as a main Center
claims.content: The Feeling Center is one of the three main Centers of human intelligence, alongside the Instinctive and Thinking Centers.

claims.title: Type Two feelings appear more visible
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two does not necessarily feel more intensely than other types; its feelings are more visible because they are shown through action.

claims.title: Type Two discomfort with verbal communication
claims.content: Enneagram Type Twos are often uncomfortable with linear, verbal forms of communication.

claims.title: Type Two strain on the body
claims.content: In unhealthy Enneagram Type Two, the Moving-Instinctual Center can be broken down by the constant strain of imbalanced feelings, and Twos may damage their health over emotional issues.

claims.title: Type Two balanced compassion
claims.content: Enneagram Type Twos no longer need to be compulsively loving once their hearts are unblocked, and they can care for themselves and others in a balanced way.

claims.title: Primary type development is revolutionary
claims.content: In the primary types, development is revolutionary and can proceed rapidly once the disconnected Center is integrated to some degree.

claims.title: Type Two develops Thinking Center
claims.content: Average Enneagram Type Twos can loosen identification with their personalities by developing their Thinking Centers.

claims.title: Type Two instincts overwhelmed by feelings
claims.content: In Enneagram Type Two, instinctual responses are overwhelmed by feelings and identifications with other people.

claims.title: Type Two unhealthy thinking distortion
claims.content: In unhealthy Enneagram Type Two, the Thinking Center becomes caught in the Feeling-Instinctual knot, causing distorted thinking, denial, rationalization, and obsessive thoughts.

claims.title: Type Two in Feeling Triad
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two is in the Feeling Triad.

claims.title: Type Two balances Feeling Center
claims.content: As Enneagram Type Twos sit with emotions without acting on them, the Feeling Center comes into balance as repressed hurts surface and heal.

claims.title: Type Two examines negative feelings
claims.content: Enneagram Type Twos can become more conscious of genuine feelings and motivations, especially negative ones, to separate emotions from doing.

claims.title: Thinking Center is inner quiet
claims.content: The Essential quality of the Thinking Center concerns developing the inner guidance of quiet mind, not formal study or scholarship.

claims.title: Type Two neglects self-care
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two becomes more identified with others' needs over time and may stop caring for itself as the pattern intensifies.

claims.title: Type Two food and medication misuse
claims.content: Unhealthy Enneagram Type Twos often abuse food or medications to act out emotional imbalances on their bodies.

claims.title: Type Two intelligence not reduced
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two's low engagement with the Thinking Center does not reflect intelligence; Twos may have strong mental capacities but rely on them less.

claims.title: Type Two compulsive talk about feelings
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two may compulsively talk about feeling reactions, including gossiping, complaining, and florid reactions.

claims.title: Type Two identifies with Feeling
claims.content: Enneagram Type Two, the Helper, identifies mainly with its Feeling Center.

claims.title: Type Two distinguishes emotions from instincts
claims.content: Enneagram Type Twos develop healthier qualities by distinguishing emotional reactions from basic instinctual responses and needs.

claims.title: Type Two difficulty with perspective
claims.content: Many Enneagram Type Twos report that emotions make it hard to find inner quiet, gain perspective, see the big picture, or connect ideas.

claims.title: Type Two feeling interferes with instinct
claims.content: In Enneagram Type Two, the Feeling Center interferes with the function of the Moving-Instinctual Center in the average range.

claims.title: Secondary type development is evolutionary
claims.content: In the secondary types, development is evolutionary, beginning more easily but proceeding at a slower pace in small steps.

claims.title: Center of a type's Triad
claims.content: Center of a type's Triad: the center where that type has the most difficulty, being most out of touch or blocked in expressing the Essential qualities of that function.

claims.title: Type Three is blocked in Feeling Center
claims.content: Personality Type Three is at the Center of its Triad, where it has the most difficulty with the Feeling Center.

claims.title: Threes mostly operate in functioning mode
claims.content: Personality Type Three mostly operates in a functioning mode that combines thinking and instinct.

claims.title: Healthy Threes integrate feelings
claims.content: Healthy Personality Type Three individuals integrate their feelings with their other functions and acknowledge their real emotional states, even when this makes them less effective or less approved of.

claims.title: Threes believe feeling blocks functioning
claims.content: Many Personality Type Three individuals report that they believe they cannot feel and function at the same time.

claims.title: Threes switch to feeling mode
claims.content: Average Personality Type Three individuals switch occasionally to a feeling mode, where they cannot function effectively.

claims.title: Threes rewarded for setting feelings aside
claims.content: Parents and other people have rewarded Personality Type Three individuals for setting their feelings aside and performing well.

claims.title: Moving decline in unhealthy Threes
claims.content: As the Moving Center declines in unhealthy Personality Type Three individuals, they may show substance abuse, self-neglect, and paralysis of effective action.

claims.title: Fours resolve Feeling Center blockage
claims.content: Personality Type Four is identified with the Feeling Center and resolves its blockage by thinking about identity and value.

claims.title: Unhealthy Threes' obsessive thinking
claims.content: When the Thinking Center is imbalanced in unhealthy Personality Type Three individuals, they develop obsessive thinking about achievements, possessions, or people they blame for their emotional problems.

claims.title: Threes avoid feelings under pressure
claims.content: As demands to perform well increase, average Personality Type Three individuals try to avoid feeling mode and return to functioning mode quickly.

claims.title: Integration lets heart qualities emerge
claims.content: As healthy Personality Type Three individuals integrate their feelings, they are less led by unconscious emotional reactions, and the Essential qualities of the heart emerge.

claims.title: Repressed feelings drive Threes' behavior
claims.content: As the split between feeling and functioning grows in less healthy Personality Type Three individuals, unconscious feelings increasingly direct their behavior, leading to compulsive acting out.

claims.title: Fours stimulate feelings through thinking
claims.content: Personality Type Four individuals use their Thinking Center to artificially stimulate their Feeling Center, which often leads to romanticism, eroticism, baroque fantasy, and stormy relationships.

claims.title: Threes' feelings are disconnected
claims.content: Personality Type Three's feelings are not properly linked with its Thinking and Instinct Centers.

claims.title: Fours use fantasy to sustain moods
claims.content: Average Fours cultivate a rich fantasy life to maintain their moods, even negative ones.

claims.title: Sixes: disconnected thinking center
claims.content: In Type Six, thinking is disconnected from the other two functions, shown by the T in a box.

claims.title: Fives: thinking spreads to other centers
claims.content: In average Fives, thinking mixes with the Feeling Center, and in unhealthy Fives, thinking also imbalances the Moving-Instinctive Center.

claims.title: Average Fives: growing emotional distance
claims.content: As average Fives become more estranged from their identity and value, they become less able to connect emotionally with others.

claims.title: Fours: missing sense fuels creativity
claims.content: For Fours, the sense that something is missing often becomes a source of creativity.

claims.title: Unhealthy Fours: blocked feeling mixes
claims.content: In unhealthy Fours, the blocked Feeling Center mixes with the Thinking Center and the Moving-Instinctive Center.

claims.title: Healthy Fours: hole fills from within
claims.content: When healthy Fours stay with the feeling that something is missing, the hole in their hearts fills from within and gives them a permanent foundation for their value and identity.

claims.title: Fives identify with thinking
claims.content: Type Five identifies primarily with the Thinking Center.

claims.title: Fives develop through grounding
claims.content: Fives develop by learning to tell thoughts from feelings and by becoming more grounded in their bodies and physical reality.

claims.title: Sixes: look outside for guidance
claims.content: Sixes have the most difficulty connecting with the quiet mind or trusting their own inner guidance, so they look outside themselves for guidance and support.

claims.title: Unhealthy Fours: suicide in worst cases
claims.content: In the worst-case scenarios, unhealthy Fours commit suicide.

claims.title: Healthy Fours: feelings without overthinking
claims.content: Healthy Fours are identified with their feelings but do not intensify them through misuse of the Thinking Center.

claims.title: Fives: compulsive thinking as compensation
claims.content: Fives compulsively think to compensate for the blockage of inner guidance and the quiet mind in the Thinking Center.

claims.title: Healthy Fives: identify with thoughts
claims.content: Healthy Fives identify with their thoughts instead of with the source and background of their thinking.

claims.title: Extremely unhealthy Fives: suicide risk
claims.content: Extremely unhealthy Fives are prone to suicide.

claims.title: Unhealthy Fours: substance and self-harm risk
claims.content: Unhealthy Fours may abuse substances or indulge in self-destructive activities to satisfy emotional cravings.

claims.title: Unhealthy Fives: neglect and isolation
claims.content: Unhealthy Fives lose awareness of basic physical needs, become isolated, and lose the ability to care for themselves.

claims.title: Fours resist releasing covering moods
claims.content: Fours have great difficulty letting go of moods that cover the perceived hole in their feelings.

claims.title: Average Fives: self-created reality
claims.content: Average Fives live in a reality of their own creation that feels more real to them than their actual lives.

claims.title: Fives: shift to quiet mind
claims.content: As Fives become more present and less identified with thoughts, their identification shifts to the spacious quality of the quiet mind.

claims.title: Sevens use movement to think
claims.content: Type Seven individuals are blocked in the quiet mind and use their moving-instinctive center to stimulate and intensify their thinking.

claims.title: Sevens seek stimulation
claims.content: Average Type Seven individuals have difficulty taking in impressions adequately, so they seek stimulating environments and experiences.

claims.title: Healthy Sixes integrate thinking
claims.content: Healthy Type Six individuals develop themselves by integrating their thinking with their other two centers rather than identifying with one function.

claims.title: Sixes rely on outside guidance
claims.content: Type Six individuals distrust their own thinking and look to outside sources for guidance, judging those sources mainly by emotional reactions and intuitions.

claims.title: Sixes in thinking mode
claims.content: Type Six individuals in thinking mode entertain many ideas but cannot integrate them into their lives or evaluate them in a balanced way.

claims.title: Sixes in duty mode reactions
claims.content: Type Six individuals in duty mode often have frequent, powerful emotional reactions that they act on, because their thinking center is not engaged to provide perspective.

claims.title: Sixes in duty mode
claims.content: Type Six individuals in duty mode are active, service-oriented, committed, and highly responsible to what they feel they must do.

claims.title: Sixes and the quiet mind
claims.content: Type Six individuals must stay present to their thoughts long enough to allow the quiet mind to emerge, which often increases their anxiety.

claims.title: Quiet mind defined
claims.content: The quiet mind is the ability to stay mentally silent so that real perceptions and inner guidance can arise.

claims.title: Sevens focus on anticipation
claims.content: Average Type Seven individuals are often thinking about something else while they act, with their attention focused on what they anticipate.

claims.title: Unhealthy Sixes and violence
claims.content: Unhealthy Type Six individuals may act on delusional ideas, and in extreme cases may resort to violence that is based on distorted thinking rather than personal feelings.

claims.title: Eights: feeling work for balance
claims.content: Eights would benefit from working with their feelings, and focusing awareness on the Feeling Center gives them more balance.

claims.title: Eights: discerning thoughts from impulses
claims.content: Eights can develop by discerning their thoughts from their instinctive impulses, which creates inner space, steadiness, and peace from which actions can arise.

claims.title: Eights: clarity and wholeness
claims.content: When the Thinking Center is freed from instinctive dominance, Eights can contact their own clarity and inner guidance, giving them a sense of Being, strength, and wholeness.

claims.title: Sevens: feeling as least used
claims.content: In Enneagram Type Seven, the Feeling Center is the least used part of the ego, and Sevens tend not to stay with their feelings.

claims.title: Eights: Moving-Instinctive Center focus
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight is identified primarily with the Moving-Instinctive Center, and Eights are strongly connected to physical energy, vitality, and immediate reactions.

claims.title: Unhealthy Eights: imbalance and control
claims.content: In unhealthy Eights, the Feeling and Thinking centers become imbalanced, and their passion can deteriorate into a hard-hearted quest for control and survival.

claims.title: Average Eights: shrewd strategizing
claims.content: In average Eights, instinctual energy mixes with thinking, producing a shrewd character that strategizes about safety, security, money, sex, and food and can lead to unwise choices.

claims.title: Sevens: stimulation mistaken for feeling
claims.content: Sevens often mistake stimulation, excitement, or hysteria for feeling and associate high stimulation with happiness and well-being.

claims.title: Eights: freedom through uplifting others
claims.content: Eights can find freedom from rage and grief by using their instinctual capacities to uplift others who have been victims of injustice or abuse.

claims.title: Unhealthy Sevens: mood and panic symptoms
claims.content: Unhealthy Sevens can experience major mood swings, rapid changes of affect, hysterical reactions, and panic attacks.

claims.title: Sevens: slowing thoughts for growth
claims.content: Sevens need to disengage their instincts from their thinking so their thoughts can slow down.

claims.title: Unhealthy Sevens: overstimulated centers
claims.content: In unhealthy Sevens, anxiety drives the Thinking and Moving-Instinctual centers to their limit, and the Feeling Center is also drafted to stimulate thinking.

claims.title: Sevens: fulfillment from persistence
claims.content: Sevens who persist in the quieting process become open to the magnificence of reality and find the fulfillment they have sought.

claims.title: Sevens: anxiety while quieting thoughts
claims.content: Quieting thoughts often causes Sevens anxiety because they identify with thinking, but staying with the process can lead to a quiet mind that removes the need to escape into thoughts and activities.

claims.title: Eights: healing through volunteer work
claims.content: Many Eights find healing and satisfaction in volunteer work and in helping the weak and disenfranchised.

claims.title: Nines switch between two modes
claims.content: Nines function in either instinct mode or daydream mode, and the two modes are disconnected from each other to varying degrees.

claims.title: Nines stay in difficult relationships
claims.content: Average Nines may stay in harmful or difficult relationships to keep their connection to the other person's strength and energy.

claims.title: Nines grow numb and apathetic
claims.content: As disengagement continues, Nines become increasingly numb, fatigued, and apathetic.

claims.title: Nine instinct mode definition
claims.content: Instinct mode is a Nine state of rest or routine activity in which thinking and feeling do not actively take part and the body simply performs.

claims.title: One ego tied to blockage
claims.content: The ego of Type One is primarily identified with a blockage or constriction of the Moving-Instinctive Center.

claims.title: Nine daydream mode definition
claims.content: Daydream mode is a Nine state of thinking and feeling disconnected from instinctive energy, in which all experiences feel equally stimulating and meaningful.

claims.title: Ones use emotional energy
claims.content: Ones draw on emotional energy to motivate action, and anger results from mixing emotional and instinctual energy.

claims.title: Ones need sustained anger
claims.content: Once identified with this pattern, Ones need to stay angry and irritated to compensate for a felt lack of substantiality.

claims.title: Nine anger transmuted by awareness
claims.content: Nines must let instinctive energy, especially anger, enter consciousness, where awareness transmutes it into Essential power and stability.

claims.title: Ones act through emotional reactions
claims.content: Average Ones cannot act without subconscious emotional reactions interfering, and cannot feel their feelings without acting on them.

claims.title: Nine merging versus autonomy conflict
