claims.content: Nines want to merge with others to gain vitality, but their ego structure is set up to maintain their autonomy.

claims.title: Nines merge imaginatively with others
claims.content: Average Nines merge with others in their imaginations and may neglect their real relationships with those people.

claims.title: Moving-Instinctive Center definition
claims.content: The Moving-Instinctive Center is a personality center, represented by the letter M, that is linked to instinctual energy.

claims.title: Nine daydream projects stall
claims.content: Nines in daydream mode can develop projects and creative ideas but struggle to advance them without instinctive energy.

claims.title: Nines quiet instinctual energy
claims.content: Average Nines quickly quiet arising instinctual energy and return to their usual disengagement.

claims.title: Quieting mind aids Ones
claims.content: Quieting the mind helps Enneagram Type Ones see the relative nature of their opinions and find more flexible ways of communicating.

claims.title: Ones' philosophy defends actions
claims.content: Enneagram Type One's philosophy of life defends and supports their actions rather than opening them to new possibilities.

claims.title: Ones' opinions arise from instinct
claims.content: Enneagram Type Ones often see themselves as rational, but their strong opinions usually arise from emotional and instinctive impulses rather than from the Thinking Center.

claims.title: Withdrawn types lack instinct
claims.content: Withdrawn Enneagram Types Four, Five, and Nine have the Instinctive Center as their undeveloped third Center.

claims.title: Average Ones feel guilt
claims.content: Average Enneagram Type Ones feel guilty when they violate their principles, even in minor ways.

claims.title: Unhealthy Ones rationalize behavior
claims.content: Unhealthy Enneagram Type Ones rationalize compulsive and contradictory behavior that they would condemn in others.

claims.title: Ones discern emotional responses
claims.content: Enneagram Type Ones can learn to discern their emotional responses from their instinctual impulses.

claims.title: Quieting mind reduces judgment
claims.content: Quieting the mind helps Enneagram Type Ones dispel inner judgment and criticism and discern appropriate courses of action.

claims.title: Compliant types lack thinking
claims.content: Compliant Enneagram Types One, Two, and Six have the Thinking Center as their undeveloped third Center.

claims.title: Type One center pattern
claims.content: Enneagram Type One identifies primarily with the Instinctive Center, scrambles with the Feeling Center in the average range, and imbalances the Thinking Center in the unhealthy range.

claims.title: Ones prefer practical ideas
claims.content: Ones are doers who prefer practical ideas and do not usually pursue open-ended inquiry or knowledge without a practical result.

claims.title: Imbalance of Centers table
claims.content: In the Enneagram, the Imbalance of Centers table lists for each type the Center it identifies with, the Center it scrambles with in the average range, and the Center its pattern imbalances in the unhealthy range.

claims.title: Assertive types: undeveloped Feeling Center
claims.content: Assertive Types (Three, Seven, and Eight) have the Feeling Center as their third, undeveloped Center.

claims.title: Ego inflation replaces heart identity
claims.content: Ego inflation through accomplishment, winning, and status replaces the authentic value and identity that the heart alone can give.

claims.title: Assertive types: open the heart
claims.content: The background practice for Assertive types (Threes, Sevens, and Eights) is to open the heart.

claims.title: Primary types share one Center
claims.content: For the Primary types (Threes, Sixes, and Nines), the background practice and secondary focus are on the same Center.

claims.title: Third Center alone limits growth
claims.content: Working only on the third Center may stabilize a person functioning in the average range but generally does not sustain further development toward Essential realization.

claims.title: Assertive types use intense activity
claims.content: Assertive Types compensate for their weak connection to the Feeling Center by using intense activity for stimulation, which replaces being open to and affected by experience.

claims.title: Unhealthy range needs a therapist
claims.content: For people in the unhealthy range, the suggested strategies are less helpful, and a therapist or other surrogate Center is needed for proper support.

claims.title: Compliant types: quiet the mind
claims.content: The background practice for Compliant types (Ones, Twos, and Sixes) is to work with the quiet mind.

claims.title: Feeling Center defined
claims.content: The Feeling Center, also called the heart, enables a person to be touched and affected by experience and gives a sense of value and identity through connection with self and others.

claims.title: Harmonic Group defined
claims.content: The Harmonic Group gives each type a secondary therapeutic focal point needed to unscramble the personality knot.

claims.title: Competency Group: open feelings
claims.content: The secondary practice for the Competency Group (Ones, Threes, and Fives) is opening up their feelings, using moments of grief and release of blocked feelings.

claims.title: Awareness harmonizes the Centers
claims.content: Awareness alone has the power to activate and harmonize the Centers.

claims.title: Third Center work adds stability
claims.content: Fortifying the third Center by using it properly is part of general maintenance and growth, and it gives greater stability.

claims.title: Withdrawn types: engage the body
claims.content: The background practice for Withdrawn types (Fours, Fives, and Nines) is to engage the body.

claims.title: Second Center needed for breakthroughs
claims.content: Lasting breakthroughs for people functioning in the average range require focusing on the second Center.

claims.title: Unhealthy people need three-Center support
claims.content: In unhealthy people, all three Centers are imbalanced and drawn into the defensive structure, so therapeutic support must address all three Centers.

claims.title: Positive Outlook Group: ground in body
claims.content: The secondary practice for the Positive Outlook Group (Twos, Sevens, and Nines) is grounding in the physical body and releasing energy locked there through direct experience of bodily sensations.

claims.title: Reactive Group: reframe thinking
claims.content: The secondary practice for the Reactive Group (Fours, Sixes, and Eights) is quieting the mind and reframing thinking and perceptions, with growth triggered by seeing distortions in perception and interpretation.

claims.title: Hornevian Group defined
claims.content: The Hornevian Group gives each type a background practice based on developing one of the three Centers.

claims.title: Higher Centers follow lower balance
claims.content: Higher Intellectual and Emotional Centers break through and transform awareness only after the lower Centers are unscrambled and balanced.

claims.title: Traits of a three-Centered person
claims.content: A three-Centered person is grounded and autonomous, open-hearted, and able to respond to the needs of a situation rather than driven by unconscious deficiency or fear.

claims.title: Centers alignment and health
claims.content: A person's mental and emotional health, and their degree of self-realization, depend on unscrambling and aligning the three Centers.

claims.title: Presence unifies the three Centers
claims.content: Presence is the medium in which the three Centers can be unified, and it is the basis of inner work.

claims.title: Higher Centers defined
claims.content: Higher Centers are the centers of higher intelligence and grace, called baraka by the Sufis, that can act on a person whose three Centers are aligned.

claims.title: Instinctive Center: grounding presence
claims.content: The Instinctive Center grounds presence by keeping a person conscious of the body and of the being having the experience.

claims.title: Ego cannot unify the Centers
claims.content: The ego, being partial, cannot create wholeness, so a person must show up with Presence to be worked on by grace.

claims.title: Objectivity requires all three Centers
claims.content: A person is objective and in contact with reality only after engaging all three Centers, while one scrambled Center alone limits perspective.

claims.title: Thinking Center: openness and allowing
claims.content: The Thinking Center, when functioning rightly, brings openness and allowing, so the mind quiets and lets impressions occur without inner chatter.

claims.title: Three Centers defined
claims.content: The three Centers of human intelligence are the Thinking Center, the Feeling Center, and the Instinctive Center.

claims.title: Almaas on the Centers and Essential Self
claims.content: A. H. Almaas, a spiritual teacher, has written that each Center brings a quality necessary for realizing the Essential Self.

claims.title: Feeling Center: tasting experience
claims.content: The Feeling Center tastes experience, enabling a person to engage fully with it, and it is the part of a person that loves the truth.

claims.title: Essence as source of awareness
claims.content: Essence is a quiet spaciousness beyond the distortions of fixation, and it is the source of awareness from which everything arises.

claims.title: Gunderson on documenting character types
claims.content: John G. Gunderson, M.D., stated that recognizing the universality of character types and documenting them is the single most important accomplishment of DSM-III.

claims.title: Nine Levels support trait continua
claims.content: The Enneagram's Continuum of nine Levels of Development provides evidence that traits and their disordered counterparts exist on continua.

claims.title: Enneagram and DSM-IV correspondence
claims.content: The authors examine how the Enneagram corresponds with the personality disorders cataloged in DSM-IV.

claims.title: Gunderson on DSM-III multiaxial format
claims.content: John G. Gunderson, M.D., stated that the main virtue of DSM-III is its multiaxial format, which allows better study of the relationships between personality and symptoms.

claims.title: DSM-IV definition and purpose
claims.content: DSM-IV stands for the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fourth edition, the primary reference work for mental health professionals.

claims.title: Enneagram as multiaxial typology
claims.content: The Enneagram is a multiaxial typology that can accommodate all personality disorders and neurotic disorders presented in DSM-IV while correlating personality types with them.

claims.title: Disorders can progress or coexist
claims.content: A person may move from a Level 6 personality disorder to a Level 8 disorder over time, and disorders at Levels 7 and 8 may exist at the same time.

claims.title: Levels aid therapist assessment
claims.content: Understanding personality disorders as part of a type's Levels of Development helps therapists assess a patient's past difficulties, present condition, and future prognosis.

claims.title: Personality disorders defined
claims.content: Personality traits become personality disorders only when they are inflexible and maladaptive and cause significant functional impairment or subjective distress.

claims.title: Personality traits defined
claims.content: Personality traits are enduring patterns of perceiving, relating to, and thinking about the environment and oneself, shown across many social and personal contexts.

claims.title: Disorders map to certain levels
claims.content: In the Enneagram, personality disorders correspond only to certain Levels of each personality type, not to an entire type.

claims.title: Enneagram and DSM-IV compatibility
claims.content: The author argues that correlating the Enneagram with the DSM-IV shows the Enneagram does not contradict psychiatric findings and adds context to psychiatric categories.

claims.title: Levels of Development defined
claims.content: Levels of Development are the healthy, average, and unhealthy stages within each Enneagram personality type.

claims.title: Maladaptive traits begin at Level 5
claims.content: In the Enneagram, personality traits start to become inflexible and maladaptive at Level 5.

claims.title: Incorrect correlations misattribute traits
claims.content: Incorrect correlations between disorders and Enneagram types can lead authors to misattribute the traits from which those disorders emerge.

claims.title: Disorders as parts of one type
claims.content: The Enneagram treats personality disorders as parts of a single personality type that has become unhealthy, while the DSM-IV regards them as separate disorders.

claims.title: Multiple disorders within one type
claims.content: Two or more personality disorders often appear within one Enneagram personality type, sometimes at different Levels.

claims.title: Conversion disorder maps to Type Two
claims.content: Conversion Disorder, also called Hysterical Neurosis (DSM-IV, page 452), corresponds to Personality Type Two at Level 9.

claims.title: Somatization disorder maps to Type Two
claims.content: Somatization Disorder (DSM-IV, page 446) corresponds to Personality Type Two at Level 6.

claims.title: Type Two Level 4 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 4 is The Effusive Friend.

claims.title: Histrionic Personality Disorder definition
claims.content: Histrionic Personality Disorder is a pattern of pervasive and excessive emotionality and attention-seeking behavior, beginning by early adulthood.

claims.title: Somatization Disorder definition
claims.content: Somatization Disorder is a pattern of recurring, multiple, significant somatic complaints that begin before age thirty and occur over several years, and that cannot be fully explained by a known general medical condition or a substance.

claims.title: Hypochondriasis maps to Type Two
claims.content: Hypochondriasis (DSM-IV, page 462) corresponds to Personality Type Two at Level 7.

claims.title: Histrionic disorder maps to Type Two
claims.content: Histrionic Personality Disorder (DSM-IV, page 655) corresponds to Personality Type Two at Levels 4 and 5.

claims.title: Type Two Level 6 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 6 is The Self-important "Saint".

claims.title: Type Two Level 2 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 2 is The Caring Person.

claims.title: Type Two Level 3 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 3 is The Nurturing Helper.

claims.title: Type Two Level 5 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 5 is The Possessive Intimate.

claims.title: Type Two nine levels overview
claims.content: Personality Type Two has nine Levels of Development, from Level 1 (The Disinterested Altruist) to Level 9 (The Psychosomatic Victim).

claims.title: Type Two Level 8 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 8 is The Coercive Dominator.

claims.title: Type Two Level 1 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 1 is The Disinterested Altruist.

claims.title: Type Two Level 7 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 7 is The Self-Deceptive Manipulator.

claims.title: Type Two Level 9 name
claims.content: Personality Type Two Level 9 is The Psychosomatic Victim.

claims.title: Limited recognition of others' feelings
claims.content: Individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder generally have difficulty recognizing the desires, subjective experiences, and feelings of others.

claims.title: Declining promotions from fear
claims.content: Individuals with Avoidant Personality Disorder may decline job promotions because the new responsibilities might bring criticism from coworkers.

claims.title: Sensitivity to criticism and defeat
claims.content: Individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder are very sensitive to criticism or defeat and may react with disdain, rage, or defiant counterattack.

claims.title: Shame linked to depression
claims.content: Sustained shame or humiliation in Narcissistic Personality Disorder may be associated with social withdrawal, depressed mood, and dysthymic or major depressive disorder.

claims.title: Avoidance of new friendships
claims.content: Individuals with Avoidant Personality Disorder avoid making new friends unless they are certain they will be liked and accepted without criticism.

claims.title: Grandiosity and inflated self-view
claims.content: Individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder have a grandiose sense of self-importance and often overestimate their abilities and inflate their accomplishments.

claims.title: Narcissistic Personality Disorder defined
claims.content: Narcissistic Personality Disorder is a pervasive pattern of grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy that begins by early adulthood and is present in a variety of contexts.

claims.title: Avoidance of interpersonal activities
claims.content: Individuals with Avoidant Personality Disorder avoid work or school activities involving significant interpersonal contact because of fear of criticism, disapproval, or rejection.

claims.title: Type Four Level 5 association
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four Level 5 is titled The Self-Absorbed Romantic and is associated with Avoidant Personality Disorder.

claims.title: Conditions for joining groups
claims.content: Individuals with Avoidant Personality Disorder will not join group activities unless they receive repeated and generous offers of support and nurturance.

claims.title: Type Three Level 6 association
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three Level 6 is titled The Self-indulgent Exception and is associated with Narcissistic Personality Disorder.

claims.title: Entitlement and exploitation of others
claims.content: Individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder have a sense of entitlement that, combined with low sensitivity to others' needs, may lead to conscious or unwitting exploitation of others.

claims.title: Excessive need for admiration
claims.content: Individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder generally require excessive admiration and have very fragile self-esteem.

claims.title: Intimacy requires uncritical acceptance
claims.content: Individuals with Avoidant Personality Disorder can establish intimate relationships when they have assurance of uncritical acceptance.

claims.title: Avoidant Personality Disorder defined
claims.content: Avoidant Personality Disorder is a pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation that begins by early adulthood and is present in a variety of contexts.

claims.title: Schizotypal Personality Disorder: ideas of reference
claims.content: Individuals with Schizotypal Personality Disorder often have ideas of reference, meaning they interpret casual incidents and external events as having a particular unusual meaning for them.

claims.title: Avoidant Personality Disorder: withdrawal behavior
claims.content: Individuals with Avoidant Personality Disorder are very sensitive to criticism and rejection and may withdraw from new activities or social contact.

claims.title: Ideas of reference versus delusions
claims.content: Ideas of reference differ from delusions of reference because the beliefs are not held with delusional conviction.

claims.title: Type Six levels overview
claims.content: Personality Type Six has nine levels, running from healthy Level 1 (Valiant Hero) to unhealthy Level 9 (Self-Defeating Masochist).

claims.title: Avoidant Personality Disorder: core features
claims.content: Avoidant Personality Disorder involves inhibition in social situations driven by feelings of inadequacy, low self-esteem, and fear of embarrassment or criticism.

claims.title: Type Five levels overview
claims.content: Personality Type Five has nine levels, running from healthy Level 1 (Pioneering Visionary) to unhealthy Level 9 (Imploded Schizoid).

claims.title: Schizotypal Personality Disorder: essential feature
claims.content: Schizotypal Personality Disorder is marked by pervasive social and interpersonal deficits, discomfort with close relationships, and cognitive or perceptual distortions or eccentricities of behavior.

claims.title: Schizotypal Personality Disorder: social relationships
claims.content: Individuals with Schizotypal Personality Disorder experience interpersonal relatedness as problematic, often have few or no close friends other than a first-degree relative, and prefer to keep to themselves.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 5 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 5 is the Hyperactive Extrovert.

claims.title: Histrionic craving for novelty
claims.content: Individuals with histrionic personality disorder may crave novelty and stimulation and become bored with their usual routine.

claims.title: Histrionic attention-drawing tactics
claims.content: Individuals with histrionic personality disorder may make up stories or create a scene to draw attention to themselves when they are not the center of attention.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 4 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 4 is the Experienced Sophisticate.

claims.title: Histrionic intolerance of delay
claims.content: Individuals with histrionic personality disorder are often intolerant of delayed gratification and often act to obtain immediate satisfaction.

claims.title: Histrionic intimacy difficulty
claims.content: Individuals with histrionic personality disorder have difficulty achieving emotional intimacy in romantic or sexual relationships.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 8 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 8 is the Manic-Compulsive.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 7 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 7 is the Impulsive Escapist.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 2 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 2 is the Free-Spirited Optimist.

claims.title: Passive-aggressive disorder: core feature
claims.content: Passive-aggressive personality disorder is defined by a pervasive pattern of negativistic attitudes and passive resistance to demands for adequate performance, according to DSM-IV.

claims.title: Passive-aggressive resistance behaviors
claims.content: Passive-aggressive personality disorder shows resistance through procrastination, forgetfulness, stubbornness, and intentional inefficiency, especially toward tasks from authority figures.

claims.title: Type Seven nine-level sequence
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven has nine levels, with Level 1 through Level 9 named as listed in the file.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 6 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 6 is the Excessive Hedonist.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 3 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 3 is the Accomplished Generalist.

claims.title: Passive-aggressive wavering behavior
claims.content: Individuals with passive-aggressive personality disorder waver between hostile defiance toward those they blame and attempts to win them back with apologies or promises.

claims.title: Histrionic discomfort without attention
claims.content: Individuals with histrionic personality disorder feel uncomfortable or unappreciated when they are not the center of attention.

claims.title: Histrionic disorder: core feature
claims.content: Histrionic personality disorder is defined by pervasive and excessive emotionality and attention-seeking behavior that begins by early adulthood, according to DSM-IV.

claims.title: Manic episode: symptom requirement
claims.content: A manic episode requires the mood disturbance plus at least three additional symptoms from a listed set, such as inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, or flight of ideas.

claims.title: Passive-aggressive blame of others
claims.content: Individuals with passive-aggressive personality disorder often blame their failures on the behavior of others.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 1 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 1 is the Ecstatic Appreciator.

claims.title: Histrionic vague speech style
claims.content: Individuals with histrionic personality disorder often speak in a style that is impressionistic and lacks detail, with strong opinions whose reasons are vague.

claims.title: Manic episode: mood definition
claims.content: A manic episode is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood, according to DSM-IV.

claims.title: Type Seven Level 9 name
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven Level 9 is the Panic-Stricken Hysteric.

claims.title: Antisocial disorder essential feature
claims.content: DSM-IV describes Antisocial Personality Disorder as a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, beginning in childhood or early adolescence and continuing into adulthood.

claims.title: Type Nine Level 6 disorder link
claims.content: Dependent Personality Disorder is listed in the file as associated with Type Nine at Level 6, The Resigned Fatalist.

claims.title: Type Nine nine levels
claims.content: Enneagram Personality Type Nine, The Peacemaker, has nine levels of development, from Level 1 (The Self-Possessed Guide) to Level 9 (The Self-Abandoning Ghost).

claims.title: Dependent disorder essential feature
claims.content: DSM-IV describes Dependent Personality Disorder as a pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of, leading to submissive and clinging behavior and fears of separation.

claims.title: Type Eight nine levels
claims.content: Enneagram Personality Type Eight, The Challenger, has nine levels of development, from Level 1 (The Magnanimous Heart) to Level 9 (The Violent Destroyer).

claims.title: Type Eight Level 7 disorder link
claims.content: Antisocial Personality Disorder is listed in the file as associated with Type Eight at Level 7, The Ruthless Outlaw.

claims.title: Dependent Personality Disorder: decisions
claims.content: Dependent Personality Disorder involves great difficulty making everyday decisions without excessive advice and reassurance from others.

claims.title: Discomfort during time off
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder are very uncomfortable during leisure time or vacations unless they bring work to do so they do not waste time.

claims.title: Parental type does not create child type
claims.content: The source states that the personality types of parents do not create the personality type of their child.

claims.title: Reluctance to delegate
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder are reluctant to delegate tasks or work with others, and insist that everything be done their way.

claims.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder definition
claims.content: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder is a preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and efficiency.

claims.title: Rejecting help when behind
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder may reject offers of help even when behind schedule, because they believe no one else can do the task right.

claims.title: Controlled expression of affection
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder usually express affection in a highly controlled or stilted fashion.

claims.title: Rigid standards and self-criticism
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder may force themselves and others to follow rigid moral principles and strict performance standards, and may be mercilessly self-critical about their own mistakes.

claims.title: Excessive carefulness and checking
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder are excessively careful, prone to repetition, and repeatedly check for possible mistakes.

claims.title: Rigidity about morality and values
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder may be excessively conscientious, scrupulous, and inflexible about morality, ethics, or values.

claims.title: Literal compliance with rules
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder are rigidly deferential to authority and rules and insist on literal compliance, without bending rules for extenuating circumstances.

claims.title: Type origins not fully understood
claims.content: The source states that the origins of personality type are not fully understood by science.

claims.title: No type engineering from Enneagram
claims.content: The source states that type engineering of later generations based on Enneagram information is not possible.

claims.title: Heredity and early relationships shape type
claims.content: Heredity and early childhood relationships with parents or other significant people are the two most important influences on a person's personality type, according to the source.

claims.title: Excessive household cleaning
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder may concentrate heavily on household chores, such as repeated excessive cleaning.

claims.title: Work excess over leisure
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder devote excessive effort to work and productivity, to the exclusion of leisure and friendships, and this is not explained by economic necessity.

claims.title: Parents' types cannot predict children's types
claims.content: Children born to the same parents do not reliably share a personality type, so parents' types cannot predict their children's types.

claims.title: Parenting is not decisive for type
claims.content: In the source's opinion, parenting counts for a great deal but is not the decisive factor that determines a child's personality type.

claims.title: Postponing pleasurable activities
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder may keep postponing pleasurable activities, such as vacations, so that they may never occur.

claims.title: Perfectionism causes dysfunction and distress
claims.content: Perfectionism and self-imposed high standards of performance cause significant dysfunction and distress in individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder.

claims.title: Control through rules and details
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder try to maintain control through painstaking attention to rules, trivial details, procedures, lists, schedules, or form, to the extent that the activity's main point is lost.

claims.title: Anger when control is lost
claims.content: Individuals with Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder become upset or angry when they cannot control their physical or interpersonal environment, and anger is typically not expressed directly.

claims.title: Parents shape personality, not type
claims.content: Parents usually play a significant role in shaping a child's overall personality pattern, including the Level of Development at which identity emerges, but do not determine the child's type.

claims.title: Dominant Affect Groups reveal background
claims.content: Dominant Affect Groups reveal the unconscious emotional background a person brings to all areas of life and are important for transformational work.

claims.title: High responder types named
claims.content: Eights, Sevens, and Threes are high responders with abundant energy.

claims.title: Attachment-Based Group membership
claims.content: The Attachment-Based Group includes Enneagram Types Three, Six, and Nine, which have problems with deeply held attachments to situations or states that work for them.

claims.title: Temperament fit challenge for parents
claims.content: A high responder child can be very challenging to parents who are low responders or whose neuroses leave little energy for a high-energy child.

claims.title: Three temperament response types
claims.content: Scientists classify temperament in early life as high responders, low responders, or in-between responders.

claims.title: Type does not reveal parenting
claims.content: A person's type does not indicate the quality of parenting the person received.

claims.title: Environment affects child functioning
claims.content: Parenting quality and other factors such as health, education, and resource availability strongly affect a child's level of functioning.

claims.title: Attachment defined as stable desire
claims.content: Attachment is the ego's desire to maintain a comfortable and stable relationship with people or things it identifies with.

claims.title: Level of Development measures shutdown
claims.content: The Level of Development at which a child functions measures how far the child has shut down.

claims.title: Same temperament, different levels
claims.content: Two children of the same temperament can crystallize at different Levels of Development depending on the health of their family of origin.

claims.title: Levels estimate family dysfunction
claims.content: The Levels of Development can indicate how deeply defended a child became to adapt to a family's degree of dysfunction.

claims.title: Parents affect health within type
claims.content: Parents determine how healthy or unhealthy a child is as an individual representative of their type.

claims.title: Three fundamental affects named
claims.content: The three fundamental affects in object-relations theory are attachment, frustration, and rejection.

claims.title: Temperament defined as innate structure
claims.content: Temperament is the innate and genetic structure that leads to the development of a person's type.

claims.title: Children shut down in dysfunction
claims.content: Children from dysfunctional or abusive families must shut down to the degree of family dysfunction to defend themselves.

claims.title: Hornevian Groups match responder types
claims.content: In the Enneagram, high responders correspond to the aggressive Hornevian Group, low responders to the withdrawn group, and in-between responders to the compliant group.

claims.title: Each type has a primary affect
claims.content: All people operate in all three affective states, and each Enneagram type operates primarily from one of them.

claims.title: Rejection-Based Group membership
claims.content: The Enneagram Rejection-Based Group includes types Two, Five, and Eight.

claims.title: Type Seven frustration pattern
claims.content: Type Seven pins its hopes for happiness on specific experiences, which fail to satisfy it, so it keeps moving on and is repeatedly disappointed.

claims.title: Frustration defined in Enneagram work
claims.content: Frustration in Enneagram object-relations theory is the feeling that one's comfort and needs are not being sufficiently attended to, experienced as a restless, dissatisfied, or needy self.

claims.title: Type Eight rejection pattern
claims.content: Type Eight feels it is innately bad and must be powerful and in control so others will not reject it.

claims.title: Frustration-Based Group membership
claims.content: The Enneagram Frustration-Based Group includes types One, Four, and Seven.

claims.title: Type Four frustration pattern
claims.content: Type Four becomes frustrated and disappointed when others fail to meet its unrealistic expectations of protection and nurture.

claims.title: Type Two rejection pattern
claims.content: Type Two feels it must be so good that others will not reject it, covering a sense of underlying worthlessness.

claims.title: Rejection-Based defensive pattern
claims.content: Types in the Rejection-Based Group expect rejection and offer a service, ability, or resource to prevent it.

claims.title: Type Eight antidote: open-heartedness
claims.content: The antidote for Type Eight's feeling that it must control to protect itself from hurt is self-surrendering open-heartedness.

claims.title: Type Six attachment pattern
claims.content: Type Six associates certain relationships, groups, and beliefs with its security and defends them even when they may harm it.

claims.title: Type Nine attachment pattern
claims.content: Type Nine is attached to an inner comfort zone linked to autonomy and freedom and does not want that zone changed.

claims.title: Type One antidote: acceptance
claims.content: The antidote for Type One's feeling that efforts are never sufficient is acceptance of reality.

claims.title: Type One frustration pattern
claims.content: Type One feels that nothing is done well enough and that others constantly thwart its efforts to improve things.

claims.title: Type Three attachment pattern
claims.content: Type Three adjusts its self-image and feelings to win the approval and attention of others, becoming attached to whoever validates it.

claims.title: Type Four antidote: equanimity
claims.content: The antidote for Type Four's feeling that it cannot get its needs met is self-renewing equanimity.

claims.title: Type Seven antidote: gratitude
claims.content: The antidote for Type Seven's feeling that it cannot get enough of what it wants is gratitude for what is available.

claims.title: Antidote defined in Enneagram growth
claims.content: In Enneagram personal growth, the antidote to a type's most troublesome object-relation affect is the quality that counters that affect.

claims.title: Type Five rejection pattern
claims.content: Type Five feels negligible and compensates by knowing something or having a special skill useful to others.

claims.title: Type Five antidote: compassion and clarity
claims.content: The antidote for Type Five's hoarding quest for mastery is nonattached compassion and clarity.

claims.title: Type Two antidote: self-love
claims.content: The antidote for Type Two's feeling that it is loved only for its service is to love itself and others regardless of their reactions.

claims.title: Three attitudes per affect group
claims.content: Each Dominant Affect Group has three principal spiritual attitudes that can be contemplated to anchor growth, regardless of a person's type.

claims.title: Awareness lessens dominant affects
claims.content: Awareness of dominant affects and their opposite antidotes can lessen their negative impact.

claims.title: Type Four learns from Two
claims.content: Type Four needs most to learn from Two to love oneself and others unconditionally.

claims.title: Nines' antidote: love of growth
claims.content: The antidote to Nines' comfortable complacency is their love of life and growth.

claims.title: Type One learns from Four
claims.content: Type One needs most to learn from Four to listen to and trust one's unconscious impulses and inspirations.

claims.title: Type Two learns from Eight
claims.content: Type Two needs most to learn from Eight to recognize one's own strength and claim one's presence in the world.

claims.title: Missing Piece chart overview
claims.content: The Missing Piece chart lists what each type most needs to learn from another type.

claims.title: Types 1, 4, 7: acceptance and gratitude
claims.content: Types 1, 4, and 7 should reflect on acceptance, forgiveness, and gratitude to transform their frustration.

claims.title: Seven to One produces unhealthy behavior
claims.content: A direct move from Seven to One results in average to unhealthy behavior rather than learning One's higher lessons.

claims.title: Type Eight learns from Five
claims.content: Type Eight needs most to learn from Five humility and one's true place in the larger scheme of things.

claims.title: Missing Piece defined by disintegration
claims.content: A type's Missing Piece is the quality of the type in its Direction of Disintegration, especially at healthy Level i, that the type most needs for personal development.

claims.title: Sixes' antidote: courageous self-reliance
claims.content: The antidote to Sixes' ambivalent attachment to others is courageous self-reliance.

claims.title: Type Five learns from Seven
claims.content: Type Five needs most to learn from Seven that life is a joy and the universe is benevolent.

claims.title: Health traits cannot be simply listed
claims.content: Knowing the characteristics of health helps people recognize healthy traits in themselves, but healthy traits cannot simply be listed for people to acquire.

claims.title: Three Dominant Affect Groups
claims.content: Enneagram Types 1, 4, and 7 belong to the Frustration group, Types 2, 5, and 8 to the Rejection group, and Types 3, 6, and 9 to the Attachment group.

claims.title: Types 3, 6, 9: authenticity and courage
claims.content: Types 3, 6, and 9 should reflect on authenticity, courage, and self-possession to transform their feelings of attachment.

claims.title: Type Seven learns from One
claims.content: Type Seven needs most to learn from One to accept life as it is and live for a higher purpose.

claims.title: Type Nine learns from Six
claims.content: Type Nine needs most to learn from Six to rely on oneself and grow in adversity.

claims.title: Dominant affects cannot be forced away
claims.content: Dominant affects stem from object-relations patterns and are basic building blocks of ego identity that cannot be removed by force of will.

claims.title: Type Six learns from Three
claims.content: Type Six needs most to learn from Three to be inner-directed and to respect oneself.

claims.title: Missing Piece is ego alien
claims.content: People in average Levels cannot claim their Missing Piece in a balanced way because its qualities are too ego alien.

claims.title: Type Three learns from Nine
claims.content: Type Three needs most to learn from Nine how to be instead of constantly doing, achieving, or performing.

claims.title: Threes' antidote: authentic humility
claims.content: The antidote to Threes' attachment to performance is authentic humility and self-regard.

claims.title: Types 2, 5, 8: regard and surrender
claims.content: Types 2, 5, and 8 should reflect on unconditional positive regard, compassion, and self-surrender to transform their feelings of rejection.

claims.title: Identifying turns positives negative
claims.content: Identifying with positive states causes them to degenerate into their opposite.

claims.title: Adaptability is not enough
claims.content: Adaptability alone is not a sole criterion for psychological health, because adaptation can signal stultifying conformity rather than growth.

claims.title: Ego uses Essence experiences
claims.content: People often use an extraordinary experience of Essence to feel more important, reinforce pride, or feel more sexually desirable.

claims.title: No resting on laurels
claims.content: Because the Enneagram's interconnected nature shows that reality changes constantly, a person cannot rest on their laurels.

claims.title: Ego resists unfolding self
claims.content: The ego tends to identify with certain states and resist the ongoing flow of the unfolding self.

claims.title: Essential qualities are available
claims.content: Essential qualities are not owned or created by a person; they are always available as needed, and flow freely when one is open and centered.

claims.title: Three balanced by Six steadfastness
claims.content: In an integrating Three, adaptability is balanced by steadfastness to commitments, a trait of the healthy Six.

claims.title: Health as ongoing growth
claims.content: There is no single prescribed state of health for everyone, nor a final state common to all; growth is an ongoing process for each individual.

claims.title: Gifts become traps when held
claims.content: Clinging to gifts turns them into traps, since holding on to positive experiences adds weight to the ego rather than refreshing it.

claims.title: Healthy traits alone insufficient
claims.content: Acquiring the healthy traits of one's type is necessary but not sufficient for a full and balanced life.

claims.title: Gurdjieff's view of Enneagram
claims.content: Gurdjieff described the Enneagram as a living symbol and a diagram of perpetual motion.

claims.title: Two empathy needs Four self-appraisal
claims.content: The Two's empathy must be counterbalanced by the Four's honest self-appraisal, or empathy may deteriorate into sentimentality.

claims.title: Eight balanced by Two empathy
claims.content: The healthy Eight's self-assertion must be balanced by the healthy Two's empathy.

claims.title: Balancing strengths in integration
claims.content: In the Direction of Integration, one strength balances another, new potentials emerge, and another capacity emerges to keep acquired strengths in harmony.

claims.title: Retain gifts by not identifying
claims.content: To retain any Enneagram gift, a person must be open to all of them while identifying with none.

claims.title: Enneagram strengths require integration
claims.content: The healthy potentials symbolized by the Enneagram are not a checklist of assets acquired piecemeal, but require dynamic integration and balance.

claims.title: Personality clings to the familiar
claims.content: The personality tends to cling to the past, the familiar, and whatever is known, so present qualities pass by.

claims.title: Enneagram as moving symbol
claims.content: The Enneagram is a living symbol and diagram of perpetual motion whose inner lines represent the movement of awareness.

claims.title: Four self-awareness needs One objectivity
claims.content: The Four's self-awareness must be counterbalanced by the One's objectivity, or objectivity may deteriorate into rigid logic.

claims.title: Interconnected Enneagram degeneration principle
claims.content: In the interconnected Enneagram, each type eventually degenerates into its opposite unless counterbalanced by the strengths of the type in its Direction of Integration.

claims.title: Way of the Monk
claims.content: The Way of the Monk, also called the Way of Devotion, works through devotion and corresponds to the Feeling Center.

claims.title: Techniques target Center qualities
claims.content: Spiritual techniques aim to bring people into contact with the real qualities of the Three Centers.

claims.title: Real qualities of each Center
claims.content: The Instinctive Center's real qualities are grounded presence, vitality, and connectedness; the Feeling Center's are authenticity, value, true identity, and real love; the Thinking Center's are Quiet Mind, receptivity, and openness.

claims.title: Way of the Fakir
claims.content: The Way of the Fakir struggles to overcome the body through mortification and focuses on the Instinctive Center.

claims.title: Hidden Fourth Way
claims.content: Gurdjieff and others have said that a hidden Fourth Way works on all three Centers at once.

claims.title: Way of the Yogi
claims.content: The Way of the Yogi, also called the Way of Knowledge, seeks inner emptiness by quieting the mind and corresponds to the Thinking Center.

claims.title: Three traditional transformation paths
claims.content: Gurdjieff taught that three traditional paths, associated with the Three Centers, lead a person seeking genuine transformation.

claims.title: Fourth Way seekers live ordinarily
claims.content: The Fourth Way is a spiritual path in which seekers live ordinary lives in the world and practice privately, rather than retreating to a monastery as on the first three ways.

claims.title: Change is unavoidable
claims.content: People change over time, either moving forward or backward, and cannot stay the same.

claims.title: Fourth Way availability conditions
claims.content: Gurdjieff said the Fourth Way becomes available and operative when the world is in crisis or when Earth reaches a shock point in its evolution.

claims.title: Knowledge alone is insufficient
claims.content: Knowledge alone cannot change a person or bestow virtue, happiness, or fulfillment.

claims.title: Requirements for real change
claims.content: Real change in life requires awareness, self-discipline, and perseverance.

claims.title: Enneagram as Fourth Way symbol
claims.content: Gurdjieff taught that the Enneagram is the symbol of the Fourth Way, and its appearance means the Fourth Way has been opened.

claims.title: Recommendations are not self-knowledge
claims.content: Enneagram recommendations are not a substitute for self-knowledge and are at best a means of priming the pump for personal growth.

claims.title: Recommendations must be personalized
claims.content: General Enneagram recommendations cannot apply to all individual cases and must be personalized.

claims.title: Enneagram as preparation tool
claims.content: The authors believe the Enneagram is a tool that can help humanity prepare for a fundamental shift in human consciousness.

claims.title: Uses of Enneagram recommendations
claims.content: Enneagram recommendations may help focus attention on typical problems and can be used in study groups, therapy, or family discussions.

claims.title: Enneagram for ego transformation
claims.content: The Enneagram can be a powerful tool for transforming the ego when combined with practices that cultivate awareness.

claims.title: Type Two avoids reminding of kindness
claims.content: Type Two people should not remind others of good works they have done for them.

claims.title: Type Two meets own needs first
claims.content: Type Two people should meet their own needs, including rest and self-care, before attending to others' needs.

claims.title: Type Three values honesty
claims.content: Type Three people should be truthful with themselves and others about genuine feelings and needs, and avoid inflating their importance.

claims.title: Type Two recommendations overview
claims.content: Enneagram Personality Type Two has ten recommendations for balancing care for others with attention to its own needs.

claims.title: Type Two helps when asked
claims.content: Type Two people should help others when asked, especially by helping them become more capable of functioning on their own.

claims.title: Type Two asks before helping
claims.content: Type Two people should ask others what they really need before doing things for them, because intuiting needs does not mean others want them met in the intended way.

claims.title: Type Two avoids buying love
claims.content: Type Two people should not give gifts or undeserved praise to win love, and should not make their help depend on how others respond.

claims.title: Type Two checks motives before helping
claims.content: Type Two people should become more conscious of their own motives when deciding to help someone.

claims.title: Type Three recommendations overview
claims.content: Enneagram Personality Type Three has recommendations for honesty, charity, and cooperation in relationships.

claims.title: Type Two avoids rescue missions
claims.content: Type Two people should avoid rescue missions, including rescuing people to earn gratitude or fixing them to become a partner.

claims.title: Type Three builds cooperation
claims.content: Type Three people can build charity and cooperation by pausing in a busy day to connect with someone they care about.

claims.title: Type Two sought out by others
claims.content: Type Two people are probably sought out by others because they can love and appreciate others for who they are.

claims.title: Type Two shares friends
claims.content: Type Two people should not be possessive of their friends and should share them with others.

claims.title: Type Two honors primary commitments
claims.content: Type Two people should honor their primary commitments, such as to spouse and children, before cultivating new relationships.

claims.title: Type Two accepts refusals of help
claims.content: Type Two people should communicate their intentions and accept a no thank you without taking it as dislike or rejection.

claims.title: Selfless love as a strength
claims.content: Loving others selflessly is an extraordinary achievement, and developing the capacity to care about others leads to doing good in life.

claims.title: Type Two avoids seeking affection signs
claims.content: Type Two people should not look for specific signs of affection from others, since others may express care differently.

claims.title: Type Three: check acclaim expectations
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people should be aware that unrealistic expectations of acclaim can cause problems in their careers and relationships.

claims.title: Type Four recommendations list
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four has a numbered recommendation list covering feelings, productive work, positive experiences, and self-discipline.

claims.title: Type Four: do not equate self with feelings
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four people should not equate themselves with their feelings, because the self is not the same as its feelings.

claims.title: Type Four: work without waiting for mood
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four people should commit to productive, meaningful work instead of waiting until they are in the right mood.

claims.title: Type Three: take restorative breaks
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people should take short breaks, such as three to five deep breaths, to recharge and reconnect with themselves.

claims.title: Type Three: state personal limits
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people can avoid many traps by letting others know when they have reached their limit of understanding, ability, or endurance.

claims.title: Type Three: discover own core values
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people should resist adjusting to others' expectations and should invest time in discovering their own core values.

claims.title: Type Three: use energy for groups
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people should use their energy, humor, and organizing ability for the welfare of their groups and help members develop their best capacities.

claims.title: Type Three: focus on worthwhile work
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people should focus on worthwhile work, especially work that benefits others, and avoid comparing themselves with others.

claims.title: Type Three recommendations list
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three has a recommendation list whose visible items cover breaks, social awareness, own values, support for others, energy use, expectations, admitting limits, and spiritual development.

claims.title: Type Four: practice regular self-discipline
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four people should practice wholesome self-discipline, such as sleeping, working, and exercising regularly, which has a cumulative, strengthening effect.

claims.title: Type Three: support and encourage others
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people should give attention and admiration to others, especially when they deserve it, and should base relationships on cooperation rather than competition.

claims.title: Type Three: join non-personal projects
claims.content: Enneagram Type Three people can grow by getting involved in projects that have nothing to do with their own advancement.

claims.title: Type Four: seek positive experiences
claims.content: Enneagram Type Four people should put themselves in the way of positive experiences, even when they do not feel ready, to build self-esteem and self-confidence.

claims.title: Notice draining project involvement
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five should notice when intense involvement in projects does not support their self-esteem, confidence, or life situation.

claims.title: Social niceties blind spot
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five people can make others feel ill at ease by forgetting social niceties while focused on their own ideas.

claims.title: Accept others' intellectual limits
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five should accept others' intellectual limits without cynicism or harshness.

claims.title: Notice retreat into thinking
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five should notice when thinking and speculation pull them out of direct experience.

claims.title: Work through conflicts
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five should work through conflicts with others rather than withdraw into isolation.

claims.title: Cooperate and yield graciously
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five should be more cooperative and less of a loner, and yield to others graciously.

claims.title: Seek trusted advice on choices
claims.content: When fixation blocks perspective, Enneagram Type Five can seek advice from someone whose judgment they trust.

claims.title: Healthy calming methods
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five should calm down in healthy ways, without drugs or alcohol, such as exercise, biofeedback, meditation, jogging, yoga, or dancing.

claims.title: Type Five recommendations list
claims.content: Enneagram Type Five has eight recommendations for staying connected to experience while using mental capacities.

claims.title: Type Six recommendations list
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six has ten recommendations for handling anxiety, trust, responsibility, and reliance on outside support.

claims.title: Rely less on outside guidance
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should rely less on outside sources of guidance and draw on their own true nature for stability.

claims.title: Build trust with others
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should work on becoming more trusting and allow themselves to get close to a trustworthy person.

claims.title: Examine attitudes toward authority
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should examine their attitudes toward authority, including whether they reflexively rebel or seek it out.

claims.title: Be fair and direct
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should be fair with others and say what is on their mind, to avoid appearing indecisive or defensive.

claims.title: Others think well of Sixes
claims.content: Others probably think better of Enneagram Type Six people than those people realize, and few people are out to get them.

claims.title: Take responsibility for mistakes
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should take responsibility for their mistakes rather than pass the buck, since most people respect that.

claims.title: Observe impulses before acting
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven people should observe their impulses rather than acting on each one, and act only on those worth acting on.

claims.title: Identify stress overreactions
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should identify what makes them overreact under stress, since most feared outcomes have not come true.

claims.title: Be clear in relationships
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should take a clear position in relationships and tell people how they feel about them.

claims.title: Type Six anger and blame
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people tend to become edgy and blame others when they are upset or angry.

claims.title: Build realistic self-belief
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should develop a realistic belief in their own abilities and become grounded in their body to feel more secure.

claims.title: Listen and value silence
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven people should listen to others and appreciate silence and solitude instead of constant background noise.

claims.title: Type Seven recommendations list
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven has recommendations on observing impulses and listening to others, and the file's visible list begins there.

claims.title: Face anxiety without drugs
claims.content: Enneagram Type Six people should remember that anxiety is common and should be present to it, without using alcohol or other drugs to numb it.

claims.title: Type Eight: yield occasionally
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight should yield to others at least occasionally, since little is often really at stake.

claims.title: Type Seven: watch what they say
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven should watch what they say, avoiding saying more than they mean for effect, since this can damage relationships.

claims.title: Type Seven: cultivate depth
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven does not have to keep themselves or others up all the time, and should cultivate depth and not fear sorrow.

claims.title: Type Seven: practice gratitude and wonder
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven can access joy and gratitude by taking time to be grateful and to feel wonder at the beauty of life.

claims.title: Type Eight: practice self-restraint
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight shows true power through self-restraint, by not asserting their will over others even when they could.

claims.title: Type Eight: dependence on others
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight typically wants self-reliance but depends on many people, including employees and others needed for business growth.

claims.title: Type Eight recommendations overview
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight has a recommendation list for balancing self-assertion with relationships, covering self-restraint, yielding, accepting affection, and depending on others.

claims.title: Type Seven: check long-term value
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven should check whether a desired outcome will be good for them in the long run.

claims.title: Type Seven: no need to have all now
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven does not have to have everything at once, since tempting acquisitions and good opportunities usually remain available later.

claims.title: Type Seven: avoid uncontrolled pursuit
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven can lose the happiness they seek by pursuing every exciting possibility without adequate discrimination, because their deepest fear is of being deprived.

claims.title: Type Seven: choose quality experiences
claims.content: Enneagram Type Seven should choose quality over quantity, especially in experiences.

claims.title: Type Seven: happiness as by-product
claims.content: Making personal happiness the main goal tends to prevent lasting happiness, which usually comes as a by-product of engagement with something worthwhile.

claims.title: Type Seven: less stimulation builds trust
claims.content: Living with less external stimulation helps Enneagram Type Seven learn to trust themselves and be satisfied with what they do.

claims.title: Type Eight: accept others' affection
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight should let in available affection, because believing others are against them alienates people and does not show weakness.

claims.title: Type Nine: examine own role
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine should honestly examine its own contribution to problems in a marriage or with children.

claims.title: Type Eight overvalues power
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight typically overvalues power, and power accumulated at a cost is paid for physically and emotionally.

claims.title: Type Nine: do not repress feelings
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine should not repress its feelings, because repressed emotions can cause somatization and other physical and psychological problems.

claims.title: Type Eight: serve higher purpose
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight should serve a higher purpose than self-interest, such as family and relationships.

claims.title: Type Nine: examine going along
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine should examine its tendency to go along with others to keep the peace.

claims.title: Type Nine: exercise regularly
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine should exercise frequently to become more aware of its body and emotions.

claims.title: Type Nine: acknowledge negative feelings
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine should recognize and become aware of its aggressions, anxieties, and other negative feelings.

claims.title: Type Eight: remembered as benefactor
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight who uses power to create hope and prosperity for others is remembered as a benefactor and gains loyal allies.

claims.title: Type Nine: become active participant
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine should focus its attention to become an active participant in the world around it.

claims.title: Somatization: bodily symptoms from emotions
claims.content: Somatization refers to unexplained bodily ailments, such as headaches, backaches, and nausea, that result from repressed emotions.

claims.title: Type Eight: weigh harm against good
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight should consider the harm it can do to others and the good it can do, and decide how it wishes to be remembered.

claims.title: Type Nine recommendation list
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine has a numbered list of recommendations for attention, relationships, feelings, and body awareness.

claims.title: Type Eight: surrender to Higher Power
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight may need to surrender to a Higher Power if one exists, which is a difficult step for Eights.

claims.title: Type Eight: change lower-level course
claims.content: Enneagram Type Eight who has fallen into the lower levels and harmed others has reason to change course while it is still possible.

claims.title: Type Nine: pay attention
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine should exert itself to pay attention and not drift off, tune out people, or daydream.

claims.title: Agoraphobia: fear of public places
claims.content: Agoraphobia is a fear of going out into public.

claims.title: One: let others decide
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should allow others to be as they are and make their own decisions, rather than imposing rules or principles on every situation.

claims.title: Nine: vent anger to loved ones
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine people should trust themselves to vent their anger and fears with their spouse and friends.

claims.title: One: journal or group work
claims.content: Keeping a journal or joining group therapy or group work may help Enneagram Type One people develop their emotions and see that others will not condemn human needs and limitations.

claims.title: One: living wisdom over rules
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should let living wisdom guide them rather than rules or their sense of rightness, since listeners must be ready to hear wise thoughts.

claims.title: Nine: accept life fully
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine people should accept their lives and learn to feel the magnitude of being alive.

claims.title: Nine: avoid tranquilizers except crises
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine people should not use drugs or alcohol to tranquilize themselves, except at times of great crisis.

claims.title: Nine: crisis coping builds esteem
claims.content: Coping with crises increases the self-esteem of Enneagram Type Nine people and shows others that they can rely on them for support in crises.

claims.title: Nine: attentiveness deepens bonds
claims.content: Others will love Enneagram Type Nine people and seek them out more if they feel understood and see that Type Nine people attend to their needs.

claims.title: One: get in touch with feelings
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should get in touch with their feelings, particularly their unconscious impulses.

claims.title: One: irritation won't help others
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should not dwell on others' wrongdoings, because their irritation will not help others see another way of being, even when others are wrong.

claims.title: One: anger alienates others
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people's self-righteous anger is their Achilles' heel, because it alienates people so they cannot hear many good things Type One people have to say.

claims.title: Nine: expression won't harm bonds
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine people should have confidence that expressing themselves will not damage their relationships.

claims.title: One: listen to others
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should listen to others, because others are often right and there is usually some truth in their views.

claims.title: Nine: receptivity is an asset
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine people's receptivity to others is one of their greatest assets, because others feel calm, safe, and accepted around them.

claims.title: Type One recommendation list
claims.content: Enneagram Type One recommendations cover relaxing, patience, self-criticism, feelings, anger, letting others decide, and listening to others.

claims.title: One: have patience with others
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should have patience, since others may change later even if they do not change right away, and their words and example may do more good than they realize.

claims.title: One: expect slow change in others
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should not expect others to change immediately, because what is obvious to them may not be obvious to others.

claims.title: One: repressed anger harms health
claims.content: Repressed anger may be giving Enneagram Type One people an ulcer or high blood pressure, and it is a warning of worse things to come.

claims.title: Expressing feelings threatens many types
claims.content: Expressing feelings to others is threatening to many personality types, so Enneagram Type Nine people are not alone in finding it hard.

claims.title: Nine: listen and know people
claims.content: Enneagram Type Nine people should listen carefully to others and get to know them as they really are.

claims.title: One: harsh self-criticism undermines
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should recognize that harsh self-criticism can make them tense, nervous, and self-doubting rather than helping them improve.

claims.title: Nine: risk of unlived life
claims.content: Repressed Enneagram Type Nine people may reach the end of their lives and realize they never really lived, as if their lives happened to someone else.

claims.title: One: learn to relax
claims.content: Enneagram Type One people should learn to relax and take time for themselves without feeling that everything depends on them.

claims.title: Nine: tranquilizers dull awareness
claims.content: Using drugs or alcohol to tranquilize oneself may reduce anxiety but dulls the awareness and coping ability that Enneagram Type Nine people are trying to develop.

claims.title: Focus on real problems
claims.content: Type One readers should identify what is really bothering them and address those problems rather than spending energy on minor annoyances.

claims.title: Essence as Essential nature
claims.content: Essence is the Essential nature a person discovers through a spiritual context, which the source describes as the path to genuine fulfillment.

claims.title: Unhealthy Ones: obsessive and compulsive
claims.content: Unhealthy Type One individuals tend to be obsessive in thought and compulsive in action, and average Ones begin to show these behaviors.

claims.title: No single correct way
claims.content: There is probably no single absolutely correct way to do everyday activities, and many things can be done differently without disadvantage.

claims.title: Goodness does not require perfection
claims.content: A person does not have to be perfect to be good.

claims.title: Self-transcendence is difficult
claims.content: Self-transcendence is difficult and frightening because it requires acting in ways foreign to one's personality and past habits.

claims.title: Orderliness desire as warning sign
claims.content: A desire for total orderliness and control of one's environment is a warning sign of other, darker disorders.

claims.title: Orderliness as displaced fear
claims.content: An exaggerated desire for orderliness is often a displacement for fear of losing control in another area of life.

claims.title: Essence states are free
claims.content: States of living in Essence are marked by freedom and are dynamic and ever-evolving.

claims.title: Transcending ego requires openness to love
claims.content: Learning to transcend the ego involves learning to be open to love.

claims.title: Self-knowledge takes years
claims.content: Real self-knowledge comes only after years of patient effort on oneself, according to the book's account of Gurdjieff's teaching.

claims.title: Ego states are fixed
claims.content: Ego states are relatively fixed and unfree, involving compulsion and losing oneself in illusions and mechanical responses.

claims.title: Pickiness undermines advice credibility
claims.content: Perfectionism that is mere pickiness undermines others' confidence in one's advice about truly important matters.

claims.title: Self-change precedes external change
claims.content: Self-change is the basic prerequisite for external change in a person's life.

claims.title: Presence increases Essence support
claims.content: The more aware a person is and the more presence they use, the more Essence supports the healthy expression of their personality.

claims.title: Basic Desire found in Essence
claims.content: Basic Desire is what a person seeks, and the file says it can be found in Essence rather than in the ego.

claims.title: Essence as true nature
claims.content: Essence is a person's true nature and the ground of their being, and personality is made out of Essence.

claims.title: Liberation is gradual
claims.content: Liberation is gradual: people move up and down the Levels, and new capacities awaken as they open to their Missing Piece.

claims.title: Awareness and willingness key to work
claims.content: Awareness, including mindfulness, plus the willingness and ability to work through psychological issues are the keys to personal work.

claims.title: Personality is part of Self
claims.content: Personality is only part of a person's true Self.

claims.title: Level 1 brings contact with Essence
claims.content: Reaching Level 1, the Level of Liberation, means coming into contact with one's Essence.

claims.title: Ego cannot meet Basic Desire
claims.content: The ego cannot fulfill a person's Basic Desire, so the person must turn to Essence for it.

claims.title: Basic Desire arrives at Level 1
claims.content: People get their Basic Desire when they move to the Level of Liberation (Level 1).

claims.title: Personal work proceeds in layers
claims.content: Work on oneself proceeds layer by layer, from the most external forms of personality to the inner core of one's Being.

claims.title: Living in Essence defined
claims.content: Living in Essence means becoming a fully functioning, integrated person by transcending the limits of the ego.

claims.title: Awareness of three barriers
claims.content: People cannot transform themselves directly, but they can bring awareness to their resistance to reality, attachment to self-image, and fear.

claims.title: Disidentifying from personality
claims.content: Transformation requires disidentifying from the personality and identifying with Essence, and this cannot be done by judging, disliking, or trying to get rid of the personality.

claims.title: Work grows harder with depth
claims.content: The deeper a person goes in the transformational process, the more difficult it becomes at least for a while, because deeper pain and more subtle barriers emerge.

claims.title: Personality defined as identification
claims.content: Personality is the identifying with certain states, feelings, thoughts, and reactions, which makes a person experience themselves as less than their full self.

claims.title: Process continues for life
claims.content: The transformational process has no finish line and continues as long as a person lives.

claims.title: Personality is part, not whole
claims.content: Personality is part of a person, not separate from them; the problem is mistaking that part for the whole.

claims.title: Essence: true self
claims.content: Essence is a person's true self, which can be recognized and distinguished from the personality.

claims.title: Personality's protective function
claims.content: The personality's function is to close a person down so they feel defended against a threatening and uncertain world, which was adaptive and necessary in childhood.

claims.title: Personality imitates Essential qualities
claims.content: Personality contains imitations of Essence's expansive qualities, including joy, love, peace, compassion, strength, and understanding.

claims.title: Personality lacks inherent authority
claims.content: Personality has no authority or power in itself because it is a mental construct rather than what is real in a person.

claims.title: Psychology and spirituality are connected
claims.content: Psychological work and spiritual development are connected and are stages in the full development of a human being.

claims.title: Presence lets Essence manifest
claims.content: When a person becomes present, the automatic workings of personality cannot operate and the deeper qualities of Essence manifest.

claims.title: Personality defined as constructed identity
claims.content: Personality is a construct built from memory and imagination that operates unconsciously and depends on tension and identification.

claims.title: Each path needs the other
claims.content: Psychology without spirituality is described as arid and meaningless, while spirituality without psychological grounding leads to vanity and illusions.

claims.title: Essence defined as deeper human nature
claims.content: Essence, also called Essential nature, is the deeper qualities of a person's heart, mind, and body that manifest when the person becomes present.

claims.title: Personality focuses on past and future
claims.content: Personality is constantly reacting to the present moment, with attention focused on imagination, the future, or the past.

claims.title: Awareness changes personality patterns
claims.content: Old personality patterns change without direct effort in proportion to the depth of awareness brought to them, and the required effort is waking up and letting go.

claims.title: Essence and personality both needed
claims.content: Essence and personality are integral parts of each other, and both are necessary for self-development.

claims.title: Ordinary person's limited essence expression
claims.content: The ordinary person lacks the ability to use personality to carry out Essential wishes, so Essential impulses appear mainly as simple instinctive behavior and primitive emotions.

claims.title: Gurdjieff on typical essence
claims.content: Gurdjieff said a person's essence is often primitive, savage, childish, or simply stupid, and many essences are dead.

claims.title: Essence as the deeper self
claims.content: Essence is the deeper, Essential self that remains unfathomable to the ego mind and expresses itself through personality.

claims.title: Healthy ego before transformation
claims.content: A healthy, well-integrated ego must be developed before it can be given up in the transformational process.

claims.title: Personality as acquired habits
claims.content: Personality is the set of acquired habits and forms through which the Essential self functions in social life.

claims.title: Balance shifts toward Essence
claims.content: As a person becomes liberated from the negative aspects of personality, the balance shifts toward Essence and more of the self lives out of Essence.

claims.title: Identification with essential states
claims.content: Identifying with Essential states can create a new ego identity that claims spiritual experiences as part of the self-image.

claims.title: Essence maturity needs balance
claims.content: Development of essence to maturity depends on work on oneself and on a balance between a relatively healthy essence and a personality that is not crushingly heavy.

claims.title: Essence as growth of freedom
claims.content: The move to Essence is described as a growth of freedom from the aspects of oneself that cause unfreedom and suffering, not an escape from oneself.

claims.title: Instinctive Center work: boundaries
claims.content: Work with the Instinctive Center involves recognizing imaginary boundaries and their artificial nature, after which a person can reexperience themselves as Presence.
